We organize existing approaches into several themes, including deep generative and discriminative models, kernel and graph-based learning, online and reinforcement learning, optimization, uncertainty quantification, and data-efficient inference. We then examine applications in vision, speech, robotics, networks, computational biology, remote sensing, finance, and distributed computing. Particular attention is given to learning under limited, noisy, streaming, or partially observed data; scalable computation in heterogeneous environments; and the use of structure, geometry, and domain knowledge to improve generalization. The paper also discusses emerging risks involving privacy, security, adversarial manipulation, reliability, and fairness, arguing that these concerns must be addressed during system design rather than after deployment. Finally, we identify open problems concerning interpretability, robustness, resource-aware learning, human interaction, and the development of principled guarantees for increasingly autonomous intelligent systems.

original_abstract: The general trend in NLP is towards increasing model capacity and performance via deeper neural networks. However, simply stacking more layers of the popular Transformer architecture for machine translation results in poor convergence and high computational overhead. Our empirical analysis suggests that convergence is poor due to gradient vanishing caused by the interaction between residual connections and layer normalization. We propose depth-scaled initialization (DS-Init), which decreases parameter variance at the initialization stage, and reduces output variance of residual connections so as to ease gradient back-propagation through normalization layers. To address computational cost, we propose a merged attention sublayer (MAtt) which combines a simplified averagebased self-attention sublayer and the encoderdecoder attention sublayer on the decoder side. Results on WMT and IWSLT translation tasks with five translation directions show that deep Transformers with DS-Init and MAtt can substantially outperform their base counterpart in terms of BLEU (+1.1 BLEU on average for 12-layer models), while matching the decoding speed of the baseline model thanks to the efficiency improvements of MAtt.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a multidisciplinary review of contemporary computational methods for intelligent systems, emphasizing the interaction between theoretical foundations, algorithmic design, and real-world deployment. We organize recent work into five themes: combinatorial and network optimization; statistical learning and representation; generative and sequential modeling; efficient inference and signal or image processing; and security, privacy, and reliability. Across these themes, we examine how structural assumptions, uncertainty, resource constraints, and human objectives influence algorithmic performance. We highlight advances including adaptive optimization, deep convolutional and variational models, entropy- and information-based representations, robust network design, privacy-preserving consensus, and objective-aware generation and recommendation. Particular attention is given to evaluation: accuracy alone is insufficient when systems must also provide computational efficiency, interpretability, safety, robustness, and formal guarantees. Applications span social and biological networks, medical imaging, communications, smart infrastructure, robotics, language, and multimedia analysis. The review identifies recurring methodological challenges, including distribution shift, limited data, adversarial behavior, model instability, and the gap between theoretical and operational performance. We conclude with directions for integrating principled theory, data-driven learning, and domain knowledge into dependable intelligent systems.

original_abstract: It is generally accepted that relatively more permanent (i.e., more temporally persistent) traits are more valuable for biometric performance than less permanent traits. Although this finding is intuitive, there is no current work identifying exactly where in the biometric analysis temporal persistence makes a difference. In this paper, we answer this question. In a recent report, we introduced the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) as an index of temporal persistence for such features. In that report, we also showed that choosing only the most temporally persistent features yielded superior performance in 12 of 14 datasets. Motivated by those empirical results, we present a novel approach using synthetic features to study which aspects of a biometric identification study are influenced by the temporal persistence of features. What we show is that using more temporally persistent features produces effects on the similarity score distributions that explain why this quality is so key to biometric performance. The results identified with the synthetic data are largely reinforced by an analysis of two datasets, one based on eye-movements and one based on gait. There was one difference between the synthetic and real data: In real data, features are intercorrelated, with the level of intercorrelation increasing with increasing ICC. This increasedhttps://www.this http URL intercorrelation in real data was associated with an increase in the spread of the impostor similarity score distributions. Removing these intercorrelations for real datasets with a decorrelation step produced results which were very similar to that obtained with synthetic features.
generated_abstract: We present a data-driven framework for analyzing interdisciplinary research through heterogeneous citation networks. The framework combines semantic representations of publications with network topology, community structure, and citation-context information to identify thematic relationships that are not apparent from conventional bibliographic measures. We introduce a co-citation-based similarity matrix and use spectral methods to detect research communities, while extreme-value modeling provides statistically calibrated thresholds for identifying unusually strong cross-domain connections. The approach is designed to distinguish genuine methodological transfer from superficial topical overlap and to reduce bias caused by publication venue, background terminology, and uneven citation practices. We evaluate the framework on a corpus spanning information theory, wireless communications, statistical physics, biomedical imaging, spintronics, computer vision, and science communication. Results show that the method recovers coherent disciplinary communities while also revealing meaningful bridges between distant fields, including shared uses of optimization, stochastic modeling, imaging, and machine learning. Compared with keyword-only and standard co-citation baselines, it improves community stability and the precision of interdisciplinary-link detection. The proposed framework offers a reproducible tool for mapping emerging research areas, supporting literature discovery, and evaluating the breadth and influence of interdisciplinary scholarship.

original_abstract: Predicting surrounding vehicle behaviors are critical to autonomous vehicles when negotiating in multi-vehicle interaction scenarios. Most existing approaches require tedious training process with large amounts of data and may fail to capture the propagating uncertainty in interaction behaviors. The multi-vehicle behaviors are assumed to be generated from a stochastic process. This paper proposes an attentive recurrent neural process (ARNP) approach to overcome the above limitations, which uses a neural process (NP) to learn a distribution of multi-vehicle interaction behavior. Our proposed model inherits the flexibility of neural networks while maintaining Bayesian probabilistic characteristics. Constructed by incorporating NPs with recurrent neural networks (RNNs), the ARNP model predicts the distribution of a target vehicle trajectory conditioned on the observed long-term sequential data of all surrounding vehicles. This approach is verified by learning and predicting lane-changing trajectories in complex traffic scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms previous counterparts in terms of accuracy and uncertainty expressiveness. Moreover, the meta-learning instinct of NPs enables our proposed ARNP model to capture global information of all observations, thereby being able to adapt to new targets efficiently.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a broad review of computational methods for learning, optimization, modeling, and decision-making across emerging data-intensive applications. We organize recent work into four complementary themes: scalable statistical and optimization algorithms, learning and inference in networks, domain-specific predictive modeling, and interactive or interpretable data analysis. The review covers stochastic and distributed optimization, collaborative filtering, open-set and imbalanced classification, graph learning and adversarial robustness, network coding and wireless resource allocation, as well as surrogate modeling for evolutionary search. We also examine applications in hydrology, Internet traffic, remote sensing, genomics, recommendation, multimedia, and natural-language sentiment analysis. Particular attention is given to the trade-offs among accuracy, computational complexity, communication cost, data requirements, robustness, and interpretability. Across these domains, successful methods increasingly combine principled analytical models with data-driven learning, exploit structure such as sparsity, low rank, hierarchy, or locality, and use adaptive algorithms to cope with uncertainty and changing conditions. We conclude by identifying common methodological challenges, including reliable evaluation, reproducibility, heterogeneous and incomplete information, adversarial effects, and the transfer of models across domains. The resulting perspective highlights opportunities for unified, scalable, and application-aware learning systems.

original_abstract: An important characteristic of English written text is the abundance of noun compounds - sequences of nouns acting as a single noun, e.g., colon cancer tumor suppressor protein. While eventually mastered by domain experts, their interpretation poses a major challenge for automated analysis. Understanding noun compounds' syntax and semantics is important for many natural language applications, including question answering, machine translation, information retrieval, and information extraction. I address the problem of noun compounds syntax by means of novel, highly accurate unsupervised and lightly supervised algorithms using the Web as a corpus and search engines as interfaces to that corpus. Traditionally the Web has been viewed as a source of page hit counts, used as an estimate for n-gram word frequencies. I extend this approach by introducing novel surface features and paraphrases, which yield state-of-the-art results for the task of noun compound bracketing. I also show how these kinds of features can be applied to other structural ambiguity problems, like prepositional phrase attachment and noun phrase coordination. I address noun compound semantics by automatically generating paraphrasing verbs and prepositions that make explicit the hidden semantic relations between the nouns in a noun compound. I also demonstrate how these paraphrasing verbs can be used to solve various relational similarity problems, and how paraphrasing noun compounds can improve machine translation.
generated_abstract: We present a data-driven study of the structure, evolution, and interdisciplinary character of contemporary computational research. Using a large corpus of publications spanning machine learning, computer vision, communications, networking, systems, security, optimization, robotics, neuroscience, and the physical and social sciences, we combine citation-network analysis, topic modeling, and temporal methods to identify major research communities and the pathways connecting them. We examine how methods, algorithms, and theoretical ideas migrate across disciplinary boundaries, and distinguish influential foundational work from rapidly emerging applications. The analysis reveals a highly connected research landscape organized around a small number of transferable concepts, including representation learning, distributed optimization, probabilistic inference, graph-based modeling, and privacy-preserving computation. Interdisciplinary papers tend to combine established methods from different communities rather than introduce entirely new components, yet these unusual combinations are disproportionately associated with later impact. We also show that collaboration structure, venue diversity, and the reuse of computational tools are significant predictors of visibility and persistence. These findings provide a quantitative framework for understanding scientific development and suggest practical strategies for discovering promising connections, evaluating research portfolios, and designing policies that support productive interdisciplinary innovation.

original_abstract: In [1, 2], we have explored the theoretical aspects of feature extraction optimization processes for solving largescale problems and overcoming machine learning limitations. Majority of optimization algorithms that have been introduced in [1, 2] guarantee the optimal performance of supervised learning, given offline and discrete data, to deal with curse of dimensionality (CoD) problem. These algorithms, however, are not tailored for solving emerging learning problems. One of the important issues caused by online data is lack of sufficient samples per class. Further, traditional machine learning algorithms cannot achieve accurate training based on limited distributed data, as data has proliferated and dispersed significantly. Machine learning employs a strict model or embedded engine to train and predict which still fails to learn unseen classes and sufficiently use online data. In this chapter, we introduce these challenges elaborately. We further investigate Meta-Learning (MTL) algorithm, and their application and promises to solve the emerging problems by answering how autonomous agents can learn to learn?.
generated_abstract: Scientific literature is expanding rapidly, making it difficult for researchers to discover relevant work, assess its contributions, and understand connections across disciplines. We present a framework for learning structured representations of research articles from their text, citation links, and contextual relationships. The method combines document-level semantic embeddings with graph-based modeling of cited and citing papers, while explicitly representing entities, relations, methods, datasets, and applications. A neural encoder generates concise, informative summaries and supports citation recommendation, related-work exploration, and identification of methodological links between otherwise distant fields. To improve reliability, the framework incorporates interpretable attention mechanisms, deterministic local explanations, and checks for representational and demographic bias. We evaluate the approach on a diverse collection of scientific publications spanning computer science, engineering, medicine, biology, and the social sciences. Experiments show that exploiting citation structure substantially improves semantic retrieval and summary quality over text-only baselines, particularly for interdisciplinary papers. Human evaluations indicate that the generated summaries preserve the main contributions and limitations of source articles while reducing lexical dependence on the original text. The results demonstrate the potential of combining language modeling, graph inference, and transparent evaluation for scalable scientific knowledge synthesis.

original_abstract: We consider a variant of the classic Ski Rental online algorithm with applications to machine learning. In our variant, we allow the skier access to a black-box machine-learning algorithm that provides an estimate of the probability that there will be at most a threshold number of ski-days. We derive a class of optimal randomized algorithms to determine the strategy that minimizes the worst-case expected competitive ratio for the skier given a prediction from the machine learning algorithm,and analyze the performance and robustness of these algorithms.
generated_abstract: We present a unified computational framework for modeling, analyzing, and controlling complex dynamical systems with heterogeneous structure, uncertainty, and limited observations. The framework combines mechanistic simulation, statistical inference, machine learning, and graph-based analysis within a common workflow. Stochastic channel and multiphase-flow models illustrate how closed-form probability descriptions and validated numerical simulations can quantify local and global system behavior. Graph-theoretic and temporal-network formulations provide tools for characterizing connectivity, propagation, and intervention in evolving systems, including epidemic processes. We further incorporate deep neural operators and convolutional architectures to infer unresolved states and subgrid processes from sparse or coarse data, while enforcing conservation laws and other physical constraints. A semantic layer based on measurable probabilistic representations ensures that composed inference procedures preserve their intended distributions and supports formal validation of sampling algorithms. Across numerical experiments and application-inspired case studies, the proposed approach improves prediction, enables efficient parameter and intervention selection, and clarifies the relationship between model assumptions and observed performance. The results demonstrate that combining rigorous mathematical structure with data-driven approximation offers a flexible basis for reliable analysis of complex systems across scientific and engineering domains.

original_abstract: Typical active learning strategies are designed for tasks, such as classification, with the assumption that the output space is mutually exclusive. The assumption that these tasks always have exactly one correct answer has resulted in the creation of numerous uncertainty-based measurements, such as entropy and least confidence, which operate over a model's outputs. Unfortunately, many real-world vision tasks, like visual question answering and image captioning, have multiple correct answers, causing these measurements to overestimate uncertainty and sometimes perform worse than a random sampling baseline. In this paper, we propose a new paradigm that estimates uncertainty in the model's internal hidden space instead of the model's output space. We specifically study a manifestation of this problem for visual question answer generation (VQA), where the aim is not to classify the correct answer but to produce a natural language answer, given an image and a question. Our method overcomes the paraphrastic nature of language. It requires a semantic space that structures the model's output concepts and that enables the usage of techniques like dropout-based Bayesian uncertainty. We build a visual-semantic space that embeds paraphrases close together for any existing VQA model. We empirically show state-of-art active learning results on the task of VQA on two datasets, being 5 times more cost-efficient on Visual Genome and 3 times more cost-efficient on VQA 2.0.
generated_abstract: We present a comprehensive framework for analyzing and exploiting scholarly citation networks as heterogeneous information systems. The framework integrates bibliographic links with textual content, authorship, venues, topics, publication time, and citation context to characterize how scientific knowledge is produced, disseminated, and connected across disciplines. We formulate citation analysis and recommendation as complementary tasks: network models reveal structural properties such as influence, community formation, temporal growth, and interdisciplinary bridges, while content-based and learning-based models identify relevant papers even when direct citation evidence is sparse. To address the limitations of popularity-driven methods, we incorporate semantic similarity, novelty, citation intent, and diversity into a unified ranking objective. Experiments on a large collection of multidisciplinary publications show that combining graph structure with document representations improves citation prediction and recommendation over conventional bibliographic and text-only baselines. The analysis also demonstrates substantial differences in citation dynamics across fields, including variations in reference-list length, aging patterns, and preferential attachment. Our results provide practical guidance for scholarly search and evaluation, while highlighting the importance of transparency, privacy, open data, and field-aware metrics in the design of future scientific communication systems.

original_abstract: Neural network learning is typically slow since backpropagation needs to compute full gradients and backpropagate them across multiple layers. Despite its success of existing work in accelerating propagation through sparseness, the relevant theoretical characteristics remain unexplored and we empirically find that they suffer from the loss of information contained in unpropagated gradients. To tackle these problems, in this work, we present a unified sparse backpropagation framework and provide a detailed analysis of its theoretical characteristics. Analysis reveals that when applied to a multilayer perceptron, our framework essentially performs gradient descent using an estimated gradient similar enough to the true gradient, resulting in convergence in probability under certain conditions. Furthermore, a simple yet effective algorithm named memorized sparse backpropagation (MSBP) is proposed to remedy the problem of information loss by storing unpropagated gradients in memory for the next learning. The experiments demonstrate that the proposed MSBP is able to effectively alleviate the information loss in traditional sparse backpropagation while achieving comparable acceleration.
generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for designing and evaluating learning-based systems operating in complex, dynamic, and partially observed environments. The framework combines representation learning, sequential decision-making, uncertainty estimation, and domain-specific structural constraints, enabling models to integrate heterogeneous observations while adapting to changing conditions. We study how temporal memory, multimodal information, geometric structure, and task-dependent feedback influence prediction, control, and inference. The proposed methodology supports both centralized training and decentralized or resource-constrained deployment, and can accommodate supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement-learning objectives. We further introduce evaluation principles that consider accuracy, robustness, computational cost, interpretability, and reliability under distribution shift rather than relying solely on static benchmark performance. Experiments across vision, medical imaging, robotics, recommendation, language, and networked systems demonstrate that exploiting domain structure and explicitly modeling uncertainty consistently improves generalization and operational efficiency. The results also show that adaptive models are particularly advantageous when observations are incomplete, data quality varies over time, or multiple agents and information sources interact. These findings provide practical guidance for developing dependable learning systems beyond narrowly defined laboratory settings.

original_abstract: Indoor robotics localization, navigation and interaction heavily rely on scene understanding and reconstruction. Compared to monocular vision which usually does not explicitly introduce any geometrical constraint, stereo vision based schemes are more promising and robust to produce accurate geometrical information, such as surface normal and depth/disparity. Besides, deep learning models trained with large-scale datasets have shown their superior performance in many stereo vision tasks. However, existing stereo datasets rarely contain the high-quality surface normal and disparity ground truth, which hardly satisfy the demand of training a prospective deep model for indoor scenes. To this end, we introduce a large-scale synthetic indoor robotics stereo (IRS) dataset with over 100K stereo RGB images and high-quality surface normal and disparity maps. Leveraging the advanced rendering techniques of our customized rendering engine, the dataset is considerably close to the real-world captured images and covers several visual effects, such as brightness changes, light reflection/transmission, lens flare, vivid shadow, etc. We compare the data distribution of IRS with existing stereo datasets to illustrate the typical visual attributes of indoor scenes. In addition, we present a new deep model DispNormNet to simultaneously infer surface normal and disparity from stereo images. Compared to existing models trained on other datasets, DispNormNet trained with IRS produces much better estimation of surface normal and disparity for indoor scenes.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is increasingly applied across scientific, engineering, and social domains, yet progress is often reported through isolated algorithms, datasets, and application-specific metrics. This paper presents a cross-disciplinary perspective on the design, deployment, and evaluation of intelligent computational systems. We organize recent approaches according to their learning mechanisms, structural assumptions, optimization strategies, and operational constraints, covering biologically inspired networks, deep and multimodal models, reinforcement learning, symbolic regression, graph-based methods, and convex optimization. Particular attention is given to learning with limited or noisy data, interaction between heterogeneous modalities, exploration under sparse feedback, and the incorporation of prior knowledge. We also examine practical issues that strongly influence reported performance, including hardware-aware implementation, distributed resource management, robustness, fairness, and the absence of reliable test oracles. Drawing on representative applications in imaging, recognition, language, robotics, communications, and complex networks, we identify recurring principles and unresolved challenges. The analysis emphasizes that no single method is uniformly optimal: successful systems depend on matching inductive bias, data availability, computational architecture, and evaluation methodology to the problem structure. We conclude with recommendations for reproducible benchmarking and reliable, interpretable, and adaptable machine learning research.

original_abstract: Recently the GAN generated face images are more and more realistic with high-quality, even hard for human eyes to detect. On the other hand, the forensics community keeps on developing methods to detect these generated fake images and try to guarantee the credibility of visual contents. Although researchers have developed some methods to detect generated images, few of them explore the important problem of generalization ability of forensics model. As new types of GANs are emerging fast, the generalization ability of forensics models to detect new types of GAN images is absolutely an essential research topic. In this paper, we explore this problem and propose to use preprocessed images to train a forensic CNN model. By applying similar image level preprocessing to both real and fake training images, the forensics model is forced to learn more intrinsic features to classify the generated and real face images. Our experimental results also prove the effectiveness of the proposed method.
generated_abstract: We present a citation-aware framework for reconstructing missing scientific abstracts from the bibliographic and textual information available in a paper’s reference list. The method represents cited publications through their titles, abstracts, and inter-paper relationships, then combines topic modeling with neural sequence generation to infer the citing paper’s research problem, methodology, and principal findings. Unlike conventional summarization systems that operate on the full article, our approach is designed for cases in which only cited works are accessible, and therefore explicitly models uncertainty and conflicting topical signals. We evaluate the framework on a corpus of scientific papers spanning computer science, engineering, mathematics, neuroscience, and the social sciences by masking known abstracts and comparing reconstructed texts with the originals. Performance is measured using lexical overlap, semantic similarity, factual consistency, and expert judgments of informativeness. Results show that citation structure provides useful evidence beyond publication titles alone, while incorporating cited abstracts substantially improves identification of the paper’s domain and contributions. The generated abstracts are generally coherent and appropriately cautious, although precise numerical results and narrowly defined technical claims remain difficult to recover. We release the benchmark and evaluation protocol to support further research on citation-based scientific document reconstruction.

original_abstract: In this study, the deep learning method named reading periodic table, which utilizes deep learning to read the periodic table and the laws of the elements, was extended. The method now also learns the periodicity behind the periodic table, that is, the left- and right-most columns are adjacent to one another behind the table with one row shifted at the learning representation level. While the original method handles the table as it is, the extended method treats the periodic table as if its two edges are connected. This is achieved using novel layers named periodic convolution layers, which can handle inputs having periodicity and may be applied to other problems related to computer vision, time series, and so on if the data possesses some periodicity. In the reading periodic table method, no input of any material feature or descriptor is required. We verified that the method is also applicable for estimating the band gap of materials other than superconductors, for which the method was originally applied. We demonstrated two types of deep learning estimation: methods to estimate the existence of a band gap and those to estimate the value of the band gap given that the materials were known to have one. Finally, we discuss the limitations of the dataset and model evaluation method. We may be unable to distinguish good models based on the random train--test split scheme; thus, we must prepare an appropriate dataset where the training and test data are temporally separate.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence and computational modeling are increasingly applied across engineering, science, medicine, economics, and the social sciences, but advances are often reported in isolated communities with limited transfer of methods and insights. This paper presents a cross-disciplinary review of recent approaches spanning deep learning, reinforcement learning, probabilistic modeling, optimization, game theory, formal verification, and human-centered system design. We organize these contributions according to their principal tasks: representation and prediction, decision and control, allocation and competition, simulation, and scientific discovery. Particular attention is given to the use of pretrained models, weak or indirect supervision, domain adaptation, uncertainty, privacy, security, and meaningful human oversight. We compare the benefits and limitations of data-driven and model-based techniques, highlighting recurring issues involving generalization, interpretability, computational cost, and evaluation under changing environments. The review also identifies opportunities for combining learned representations with structural knowledge, physical constraints, and decentralized decision mechanisms. Finally, we outline a research agenda for reliable, reproducible, and resource-efficient intelligent systems capable of operating across heterogeneous domains while preserving human responsibility and supporting transparent, evidence-based decisions.

original_abstract: Online dating has become a common occurrence over the last few decades. A key challenge for online dating platforms is to determine suitable matches for their users. A lot of dating services rely on self-reported user traits and preferences for matching. At the same time, some services largely rely on user images and thus initial visual preference. Especially for the latter approach, previous research has attempted to capture users' visual preferences for automatic match recommendation. These approaches are mostly based on the assumption that physical attraction is the key factor for relationship formation and personal preferences, interests, and attitude are largely neglected. Deep learning approaches have shown that a variety of properties can be predicted from human faces to some degree, including age, health and even personality traits. Therefore, we investigate the feasibility of bridging image-based matching and matching with personal interests, preferences, and attitude. We approach the problem in a supervised manner by predicting similarity scores between two users based on images of their faces only. The ground-truth for the similarity matching scores is determined by a test that aims to capture users' preferences, interests, and attitude that are relevant for forming romantic relationships. The images are processed by a Siamese Multi-Task deep learning architecture. We find a statistically significant correlation between predicted and target similarity scores. Thus, our results indicate that learning similarities in terms of interests, preferences, and attitude from face images appears to be feasible to some degree.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a broad review of contemporary computational intelligence methods and their applications across communication networks, cyber-physical systems, graph algorithms, multimedia analysis, natural language processing, bioinformatics, economics, and autonomous systems. We organize existing approaches into four complementary themes: data-driven representation and prediction, optimization and decision making, formal analysis and verification, and distributed or adversarial computation. Particular attention is given to deep learning, probabilistic modeling, reinforcement and online learning, clustering, compressed sensing, blockchain, and message-passing methods, together with their use in problems such as caching, traffic management, face and action recognition, medical imaging, molecular prediction, and trajectory planning. We compare these techniques in terms of scalability, data requirements, interpretability, robustness, privacy, and computational complexity. The review also highlights recurring challenges, including limited or biased data, distribution shift, adversarial manipulation, resource constraints, and the difficulty of providing formal guarantees for learned components. Finally, we discuss emerging directions for combining learning with symbolic reasoning, optimization, and verification to construct intelligent systems that are adaptive, secure, explainable, and dependable in real-world environments.

original_abstract: We introduce and study the problem of Online Continual Compression, where one attempts to learn to compress and store a representative dataset from a non i.i.d data stream, while only observing each sample once. This problem is highly relevant for downstream online continual learning tasks, as well as standard learning methods under resource constrained data collection. To address this we propose a new architecture which Stacks Quantization Modules (SQM), consisting of a series of discrete autoencoders, each equipped with their own memory. Every added module is trained to reconstruct the latent space of the previous module using fewer bits, allowing the learned representation to become more compact as training progresses. This modularity has several advantages: 1) moderate compressions are quickly available early in training, which is crucial for remembering the early tasks, 2) as more data needs to be stored, earlier data becomes more compressed, freeing memory, 3) unlike previous methods, our approach does not require pretraining, even on challenging datasets. We show several potential applications of this method. We first replace the episodic memory used in Experience Replay with SQM, leading to significant gains on standard continual learning benchmarks using a fixed memory budget. We then apply our method to online compression of larger images like those from Imagenet, and show that it is also effective with other modalities, such as LiDAR data.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in systems that perceive, learn, communicate, optimize, and act in complex environments. This paper presents a broad, application-oriented survey of recent advances in intelligent systems, emphasizing the common computational principles that connect apparently diverse problems. We review adaptive and verified software libraries, deep representation learning, attention and recurrent architectures, generative and adversarial models, multimodal speech and video understanding, recommendation and search, education and healthcare, robotics, autonomous vehicles, and networked sensing. We further examine learning and optimization methods, including transfer learning, adaptive momentum, multiplicative updates, model predictive control, reinforcement-oriented resource allocation, and efficient inference. Beyond predictive performance, we discuss robustness to distribution shift, adversarial manipulation, privacy leakage, uncertainty, interpretability, and ethical responsibility. The survey also highlights the importance of formal guarantees, reproducible data management, energy-efficient hardware, and human-centered evaluation when deploying learning systems in safety-critical and socially consequential settings. By organizing these developments around shared challenges rather than application domains alone, the paper identifies recurring design trade-offs and outlines research directions for building intelligent systems that are efficient, reliable, secure, and accountable.

original_abstract: In recent years, reinforcement learning has been successful in solving video games from Atari to Star Craft II. However, the end-to-end model-free reinforcement learning (RL) is not sample efficient and requires a significant amount of computational resources to achieve superhuman level performance. Model-free RL is also unlikely to produce human-like agents for playtesting and gameplaying AI in the development cycle of complex video games. In this paper, we present a hierarchical approach to training agents with the goal of achieving human-like style and high skill level in team sports games. While this is still work in progress, our preliminary results show that the presented approach holds promise for solving the posed multi-agent learning problem.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming scientific research, engineering, communication, and decision-making, but its successful deployment requires more than improvements in predictive accuracy. This paper presents a multidisciplinary perspective on the development of reliable, scalable, and human-centered intelligent systems. We review advances in deep representation learning, graph and sequence modeling, semi-supervised learning, uncertainty calibration, optimization, and physics-informed methods, together with applications spanning autonomous vehicles, wireless and optical networks, healthcare, neurotechnology, image analysis, and cyber-physical infrastructure. Particular attention is given to learning under limited, incomplete, noisy, or streaming data; efficient computation on heterogeneous and distributed platforms; and the integration of sensing, communication, and decision processes. We further examine interpretability, human interaction, privacy, security, and adversarial robustness as essential properties for safety-critical applications. By comparing methods and design principles across seemingly disparate domains, we identify common challenges involving scalability, generalization, evaluation, and trust. The paper concludes with research directions toward adaptive, explainable, energy-efficient, and verifiably secure intelligent systems that can operate reliably in complex real-world environments.

original_abstract: This paper presents an overview of the evolution of local features from handcrafted to deep-learning-based methods, followed by a discussion of several benchmarks and papers evaluating such local features. Our investigations are motivated by 3D reconstruction problems, where the precise location of the features is important. As we describe these methods, we highlight and explain the challenges of feature extraction and potential ways to overcome them. We first present handcrafted methods, followed by methods based on classical machine learning and finally we discuss methods based on deep-learning. This largely chronologically-ordered presentation will help the reader to fully understand the topic of image and region description in order to make best use of it in modern computer vision applications. In particular, understanding handcrafted methods and their motivation can help to understand modern approaches and how machine learning is used to improve the results. We also provide references to most of the relevant literature and code.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a broad review of data-driven methods for designing intelligent, connected, and autonomous systems. It examines how machine learning, deep neural networks, reinforcement learning, graph algorithms, optimization, and probabilistic models are used to extract knowledge from heterogeneous data and support prediction, recognition, control, and decision making. Applications are discussed across healthcare, transportation, robotics, energy systems, multimedia analysis, cybersecurity, cloud computing, and the Internet of Things. Particular attention is given to methods for learning from limited, dependent, noisy, or unlabeled data; scaling computation through parallel and distributed architectures; and incorporating structural, temporal, and physical constraints into learning processes. The review also considers practical concerns that increasingly shape deployment, including interpretability, privacy, adversarial robustness, energy efficiency, and the reliability of autonomous decisions. By organizing representative approaches according to their data assumptions, computational requirements, and application objectives, the paper highlights common methodological principles as well as domain-specific challenges. It concludes by identifying open problems in trustworthy learning, adaptive systems, multi-agent coordination, and the integration of large-scale data with expert knowledge, with the aim of guiding future research toward more robust and useful intelligent systems.

original_abstract: Intrusion detection systems (IDSs) play an important role in identifying malicious attacks and threats in networking systems. As fundamental tools of IDSs, learning based classification methods have been widely employed. When it comes to detecting network intrusions in small sample sizes (e.g., emerging intrusions), the limited number and imbalanced proportion of training samples usually cause significant challenges in training supervised and semi-supervised classifiers. In this paper, we propose a general network intrusion detection framework to address the challenges of both \emph{data scarcity} and \emph{data imbalance}. The novelty of the proposed framework focuses on incorporating deep adversarial learning with statistical learning and exploiting learning based data augmentation. Given a small set of network intrusion samples, it first derives a Poisson-Gamma joint probabilistic generative model to generate synthesised intrusion data using Monte Carlo methods. Those synthesised data are then augmented by deep generative neural networks through adversarial learning. Finally, it adopts the augmented intrusion data to train supervised models for detecting network intrusions. Comprehensive experimental validations on KDD Cup 99 dataset show that the proposed framework outperforms the existing learning based IDSs in terms of improved accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.
generated_abstract: We study the problem of reconstructing missing scientific abstracts from the bibliographic and textual evidence available in cited publications. Scientific articles span highly diverse domains, from mechanism design and probabilistic inference to storage systems, imaging, formal verification, and procedural game generation, making generic summarization particularly challenging. We propose a citation-aware neural summarization framework that represents the cited titles and abstracts jointly, identifies their shared technical themes, and generates a concise description of the citing paper’s likely contribution. The model combines contextual encoding, attention, copying of domain-specific terminology, and coverage mechanisms to reduce repetition and preserve factual details. We further introduce preprocessing and evaluation procedures tailored to scientific language, including normalization of mathematical notation, technical entities, and abbreviated terms. Experiments on a collection of papers with available abstracts show that incorporating citation content substantially improves informativeness and terminology accuracy over title-only and generic summarization baselines. Human evaluation indicates that the generated abstracts capture research motivation, methodology, and principal findings while remaining readable and appropriately cautious when the available evidence is incomplete. The results demonstrate the feasibility of citation-guided abstract reconstruction as a tool for scholarly indexing, archival recovery, and literature analysis.

original_abstract: Cyberphysical systems (CPS) are ubiquitous in our personal and professional lives, and they promise to dramatically improve micro-communities (e.g., urban farms, hospitals), macro-communities (e.g., cities and metropolises), urban structures (e.g., smart homes and cars), and living structures (e.g., human bodies, synthetic genomes). The question that we address in this article pertains to designing these CPS systems to be resilient-from-the-ground-up, and through progressive learning, resilient-by-reaction. An optimally designed system is resilient to both unique attacks and recurrent attacks, the latter with a lower overhead. Overall, the notion of resilience can be thought of in the light of three main sources of lack of resilience, as follows: exogenous factors, such as natural variations and attack scenarios; mismatch between engineered designs and exogenous factors ranging from DDoS (distributed denial-of-service) attacks or other cybersecurity nightmares, so called "black swan" events, disabling critical services of the municipal electrical grids and other connected infrastructures, data breaches, and network failures; and the fragility of engineered designs themselves encompassing bugs, human-computer interactions (HCI), and the overall complexity of real-world systems. In the paper, our focus is on design and deployment innovations that are broadly applicable across a range of CPS application areas.
generated_abstract: We present a general framework for discovering and organizing scientific knowledge from heterogeneous publications. The method combines textual representations, citation-network structure, and domain-specific metadata to identify relationships among papers whose terminology, methods, and application areas differ substantially. A hierarchical neural architecture jointly learns document, author, venue, and concept representations, while an attention mechanism highlights the passages and cited works most relevant to a query. To improve robustness in low-resource settings, we incorporate subword and multilingual representations, adversarial multi-task learning, and weak supervision derived from citation contexts. The framework supports several tasks, including related-paper retrieval, citation recommendation, research-topic classification, and generation of concise literature summaries. We evaluate it on collections spanning machine learning, wireless communication, computational biology, mathematics, computer vision, and the social sciences. Compared with content-only and graph-only baselines, the combined model improves retrieval precision and citation prediction, particularly for interdisciplinary papers and emerging topics with limited citation history. Qualitative analyses show that the learned representations capture both methodological similarity and application-level connections. The results demonstrate that integrating language and scholarly-network evidence can provide more accurate, interpretable, and scalable support for literature analysis.

original_abstract: Mesh models are a promising approach for encoding the structure of 3D objects. Current mesh reconstruction systems predict uniformly distributed vertex locations of a predetermined graph through a series of graph convolutions, leading to compromises with respect to performance or resolution. In this paper, we argue that the graph representation of geometric objects allows for additional structure, which should be leveraged for enhanced reconstruction. Thus, we propose a system which properly benefits from the advantages of the geometric structure of graph encoded objects by introducing (1) a graph convolutional update preserving vertex information; (2) an adaptive splitting heuristic allowing detail to emerge; and (3) a training objective operating both on the local surfaces defined by vertices as well as the global structure defined by the mesh. Our proposed method is evaluated on the task of 3D object reconstruction from images with the ShapeNet dataset, where we demonstrate state of the art performance, both visually and numerically, while having far smaller space requirements by generating adaptive meshes
generated_abstract: This paper presents a unified perspective on the design of intelligent, networked systems that must learn from heterogeneous data while operating under resource, privacy, and reliability constraints. We review representative advances in deep learning, graph-based inference, distributed optimization, multimodal perception, anomaly detection, and privacy-preserving computation, emphasizing the common methodological challenges shared across application domains. These challenges include learning from weak, noisy, or incomplete supervision; adapting models across changing environments; representing uncertainty; coordinating decisions over multilayer networks; and deploying computation on constrained devices. We propose a framework organized around three complementary principles: data-efficient representation learning, structure-aware reasoning, and dependable system-level deployment. The framework highlights how relational information, domain knowledge, and feedback from the operating environment can improve both accuracy and robustness. We further discuss evaluation practices, scalability, communication efficiency, interpretability, and protection of sensitive information. By connecting developments that are often studied separately, the paper identifies promising directions for building adaptive systems that are efficient, transparent, and resilient in real-world settings. The resulting agenda is intended to support interdisciplinary research spanning artificial intelligence, communications, cybersecurity, robotics, and complex socio-technical systems.

original_abstract: Data science is labor-intensive and human experts are scarce but heavily involved in every aspect of it. This makes data science time consuming and restricted to experts with the resulting quality heavily dependent on their experience and skills. To make data science more accessible and scalable, we need its democratization. Automated Data Science (AutoDS) is aimed towards that goal and is emerging as an important research and business topic. We introduce and define the AutoDS challenge, followed by a proposal of a general AutoDS framework that covers existing approaches but also provides guidance for the development of new methods. We categorize and review the existing literature from multiple aspects of the problem setup and employed techniques. Then we provide several views on how AI could succeed in automating end-to-end AutoDS. We hope this survey can serve as insightful guideline for the AutoDS field and provide inspiration for future research.
generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for discovering and organizing knowledge across heterogeneous scientific literature. The approach combines semantic representations of publications with citation-network structure, enabling documents from substantially different domains to be compared, clustered, and connected according to both textual content and scholarly influence. A graph-based ranking procedure identifies influential papers, emerging themes, and bridging publications that link otherwise separated research communities. To improve reliability, the framework incorporates data-integrity checks, confidence estimates, and perturbation-based analyses that reveal sensitivity to noisy metadata and unintended biases. It also supports weakly supervised and few-shot learning, reducing dependence on manually labeled training data while retaining the ability to adapt to new disciplines. We evaluate the method on a diverse collection spanning mathematics, computer science, engineering, medicine, and social applications. Results show improved retrieval of relevant publications, more coherent thematic clusters, and more accurate identification of interdisciplinary connections than text-only and citation-only baselines. The framework offers a scalable basis for literature discovery, review, and research assessment, while emphasizing transparent evidence trails and caution against treating automated rankings as substitutes for expert judgment.

original_abstract: Recent developments in neural language models (LMs) have raised concerns about their potential misuse for automatically spreading misinformation. In light of these concerns, several studies have proposed to detect machine-generated fake news by capturing their stylistic differences from human-written text. These approaches, broadly termed stylometry, have found success in source attribution and misinformation detection in human-written texts. However, in this work, we show that stylometry is limited against machine-generated misinformation. While humans speak differently when trying to deceive, LMs generate stylistically consistent text, regardless of underlying motive. Thus, though stylometry can successfully prevent impersonation by identifying text provenance, it fails to distinguish legitimate LM applications from those that introduce false information. We create two benchmarks demonstrating the stylistic similarity between malicious and legitimate uses of LMs, employed in auto-completion and editing-assistance settings. Our findings highlight the need for non-stylometry approaches in detecting machine-generated misinformation, and open up the discussion on the desired evaluation benchmarks.
generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for designing and deploying data-driven computational methods across scientific, engineering, and cyber-physical applications. The framework separates problem representation, inference, decision making, and adaptation, allowing domain-specific models and algorithms to be combined without redesigning the entire system. It supports structured and unstructured data, discrete and continuous variables, uncertainty, partial observability, and changing environments. Learning components may exploit demonstrations, simulations, pretrained models, or physical constraints, while optimization and probabilistic inference provide efficient solutions and quantifiable guarantees. We further introduce reusable interfaces for integrating learned representations with control, diagnosis, security, and resource allocation modules. The approach is evaluated on a diverse collection of tasks, including language understanding, image and biomedical analysis, robotic manipulation, networked systems, distributed storage, smart grids, and adversarial security. Results show that modular representations improve accuracy, computational efficiency, robustness, and transfer across tasks compared with separately engineered baselines. The study also identifies important limitations, including dependence on data quality, distribution shift, interpretability, and the difficulty of obtaining formal guarantees for learned components. These findings support a general methodology for building reliable intelligent systems from interoperable computational components.

original_abstract: Real-noise denoising is a challenging task because the statistics of real-noise do not follow the normal distribution, and they are also spatially and temporally changing. In order to cope with various and complex real-noise, we propose a well-generalized denoising architecture and a transfer learning scheme. Specifically, we adopt an adaptive instance normalization to build a denoiser, which can regularize the feature map and prevent the network from overfitting to the training set. We also introduce a transfer learning scheme that transfers knowledge learned from synthetic-noise data to the real-noise denoiser. From the proposed transfer learning, the synthetic-noise denoiser can learn general features from various synthetic-noise data, and the real-noise denoiser can learn the real-noise characteristics from real data. From the experiments, we find that the proposed denoising method has great generalization ability, such that our network trained with synthetic-noise achieves the best performance for Darmstadt Noise Dataset (DND) among the methods from published papers. We can also see that the proposed transfer learning scheme robustly works for real-noise images through the learning with a very small number of labeled data.
generated_abstract: We present a computational framework for mapping the rapidly expanding landscape of artificial intelligence and data-driven research across disciplines. original_abstract: Fine-tuning a deep network trained with the standard cross-entropy loss is a strong baseline for few-shot learning. When fine-tuned transductively, this outperforms the current state-of-the-art on standard datasets such as Mini-Imagenet, Tiered-Imagenet, CIFAR-FS and FC-100 with the same hyper-parameters. The simplicity of this approach enables us to demonstrate the first few-shot learning results on the Imagenet-21k dataset. We find that using a large number of meta-training classes results in high few-shot accuracies even for a large number of test classes. We do not advocate our approach as the solution for few-shot learning, but simply use the results to highlight limitations of current benchmarks and few-shot protocols. We perform extensive studies on benchmark datasets to propose a metric that quantifies the "hardness" of a test episode. This metric can be used to report the performance of few-shot algorithms in a more systematic way.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a multidisciplinary survey of computational methods for learning, optimization, inference, and secure decision making in complex systems. The survey covers representation learning, topic models, spectral methods, variational inference, reinforcement learning, evolutionary and threshold-based optimization, and approximation techniques for large-scale search. Particular attention is given to practical constraints, including limited computation, partial observability, noisy measurements, adversarial inputs, privacy risks, and the need for formal guarantees. By comparing algorithmic assumptions, scalability, robustness, and evaluation practices across fields, we identify recurring design principles and unresolved challenges. The resulting perspective highlights opportunities for combining statistical learning with symbolic reasoning, local access models, hardware-aware computation, and human-centered interaction in future intelligent systems.

original_abstract: Deep neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples - small input perturbations that result in incorrect predictions. We study this problem in the context of models of source code, where we want the network to be robust to source-code modifications that preserve code functionality. We define a natural notion of robustness, $k$-transformation robustness, in which an adversary performs up to $k$ semantics-preserving transformations to an input program. We show how to train robust models using an adversarial training objective inspired by that of Madry et al. (2018) for continuous domains. #R##N#We implement an extensible framework for adversarial training over source code, and conduct a thorough evaluation on a number of datasets and two different architectures. Our results show (1) the increase in robustness following adversarial training, (2) the ability of training on weak adversaries to provide robustness to attacks by stronger adversaries, and (3) the shift in attribution focus of adversarially trained models towards semantic vs. syntactic features.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning now support applications spanning perception, prediction, decision making, communication, and human–computer interaction. Across these areas, we identify recurring challenges: limited or biased training data, domain shift, temporal and compositional reasoning, computational and energy constraints, uncertainty, privacy, security, and the need for interpretable and trustworthy decisions. We compare strategies for data augmentation, representation learning, model compression, attention, multimodal fusion, structured memory, and human-centered interface design. The review further highlights the importance of evaluation beyond in-domain accuracy, including cross-dataset generalization, robustness to adversarial or malicious behavior, safety, usability, and societal impact. We conclude by outlining research directions toward efficient, transparent, adaptive, and reliable intelligent systems that can operate in complex real-world environments.

original_abstract: While stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and variants have been surprisingly successful for training deep nets, several aspects of the optimization dynamics and generalization are still not well understood. In this paper, we present new empirical observations and theoretical results on both the optimization dynamics and generalization behavior of SGD for deep nets based on the Hessian of the training loss and associated quantities. We consider three specific research questions: (1) what is the relationship between the Hessian of the loss and the second moment of stochastic gradients (SGs)? (2) how can we characterize the stochastic optimization dynamics of SGD with fixed and adaptive step sizes and diagonal pre-conditioning based on the first and second moments of SGs? and (3) how can we characterize a scale-invariant generalization bound of deep nets based on the Hessian of the loss, which by itself is not scale invariant? We shed light on these three questions using theoretical results supported by extensive empirical observations, with experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10, with different batch sizes, and with different difficulty levels by synthetically adding random labels.
generated_abstract: We present an adaptive framework for deploying deep learning applications on resource-constrained mobile and edge devices. The framework jointly considers accuracy, latency, energy consumption, privacy, and communication cost, and dynamically selects sensing, inference, and transmission actions according to the current environment and application requirements. The approach supports object detection and tracking, image enhancement, and multimodal perception, while allowing models and processing stages to be distributed across end devices and edge servers. We formulate the resulting decision process as a constrained sequential optimization problem and develop a deep reinforcement learning solution with uncertainty-aware rewards. Experiments on public vision benchmarks and real mobile platforms show that adaptive execution substantially reduces energy use and network traffic while preserving or improving task accuracy. Compared with continuous full-model inference, the proposed method achieves up to 70% lower energy consumption and significant latency reductions, demonstrating the practicality of resource-aware intelligent sensing for mobile and Internet-of-Things applications.

original_abstract: Research communications often introduce biases or misrepresentations without providing reliable links to the research they use so readers can check the veracity of the claims being made. We tested the feasibility of a tool that can be used to automatically recommend research articles to research communications. From 207,538 vaccination-related PubMed articles, we selected 3,573 unique links to webpages using Altmetric. We tested a method for ranking research articles relative to each webpage using a canonical correlation analysis (CCA) approach. Outcome measures were the median rank of the correct source article; the percentage of webpages for which the source article was correctly ranked first; and the percentage ranked within the top 50 candidate articles. The best of the baseline approaches ranked the matching source article first for more a quarter of webpages; and within the top 50 for more than half. Augmenting baseline methods with CCA improved results but failed when added to some of the baseline approaches. The best CCA-based approach ranked the matching source articles first for 14%; and in the top 50 for 38%. Tools to help people identify source articles for vaccination-related research communications are potentially feasible and may support the prevention of bias and misrepresentation of research in news and social media.
generated_abstract: Deep learning has emerged as a versatile framework for addressing complex optimization, perception, and language-processing problems across heterogeneous application domains. This paper reviews recent data-driven approaches that employ neural architectures to overcome limitations of conventional model-based and feature-engineered methods. We further analyze convolutional methods for extracting biomedical relations from sparse clinical text through the fusion of multiple word representations, as well as hierarchical attention mechanisms for generating topical and contextually relevant conversational responses. Across these studies, we identify recurring design principles, including effective use of domain knowledge, multiscale or multichannel representations, intermediate supervision, attention to contextual information, and task-specific evaluation. The review highlights the benefits and remaining challenges of deploying deep learning in real-world environments, including data quality, interpretability, computational cost, generalization, and reliable evaluation. It concludes with directions for developing more robust, efficient, and application-aware intelligent systems.

original_abstract: Designing a lightweight semantic segmentation network often requires researchers to find a trade-off between performance and speed, which is always empirical due to the limited interpretability of neural networks. In order to release researchers from these tedious mechanical trials, we propose a Graph-guided Architecture Search (GAS) pipeline to automatically search real-time semantic segmentation networks. Unlike previous works that use a simplified search space and stack a repeatable cell to form a network, we introduce a novel search mechanism with new search space where a lightweight model can be effectively explored through the cell-level diversity and latencyoriented constraint. Specifically, to produce the cell-level diversity, the cell-sharing constraint is eliminated through the cell-independent manner. Then a graph convolution network (GCN) is seamlessly integrated as a communication mechanism between cells. Finally, a latency-oriented constraint is endowed into the search process to balance the speed and performance. Extensive experiments on Cityscapes and CamVid datasets demonstrate that GAS achieves new state-of-the-art trade-off between accuracy and speed. In particular, on Cityscapes dataset, GAS achieves the new best performance of 73.3% mIoU with speed of 102 FPS on Titan Xp.
generated_abstract: We present a data-driven framework for learning and analyzing dynamical systems from limited, noisy observations. Information criteria and stability constraints then rank competing models and reject descriptions that fit observations but generalize poorly. The framework supports partially observed systems, heterogeneous sampling, and singular or nearly singular numerical problems through robust preprocessing and stabilized iterative solvers. We further develop extensions for stochastic dynamics and networked systems, allowing interactions among agents, spatially distributed states, and switching regimes to be inferred from a single trajectory or multiple short experiments. Experiments on benchmark nonlinear systems and applications in epidemiology, power networks, transportation, and biological processes show that the method accurately recovers system structure, predicts future behavior, and identifies dominant mechanisms with substantially fewer samples than conventional black-box approaches. The results demonstrate that combining sparsity, physical constraints, and modern optimization provides an effective alternative to purely neural forecasting models.

original_abstract: We introduce PlatonicGAN to discover the 3D structure of an object class from an unstructured collection of 2D images, i.e., where no relation between photos is known, except that they are showing instances of the same category. The key idea is to train a deep neural network to generate 3D shapes which, when rendered to images, are indistinguishable from ground truth images (for a discriminator) under various camera poses. Discriminating 2D images instead of 3D shapes allows tapping into unstructured 2D photo collections instead of relying on curated (e.g., aligned, annotated, etc.) 3D data sets. To establish constraints between 2D image observation and their 3D interpretation, we suggest a family of rendering layers that are effectively differentiable. This family includes visual hull, absorption-only (akin to x-ray), and emission-absorption. We can successfully reconstruct 3D shapes from unstructured 2D images and extensively evaluate PlatonicGAN on a range of synthetic and real data sets achieving consistent improvements over baseline methods. We further show that PlatonicGAN can be combined with 3D supervision to improve on and in some cases even surpass the quality of 3D-supervised methods.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is increasingly used to address problems involving heterogeneous data, dynamic environments, and resource constraints, but progress remains fragmented across application domains. We then discuss adaptive learning in changing environments, including online ensembles, mean-field methods, federated optimization, dynamic network inference, and learning-assisted planning. Applications span healthcare, migration, energy poverty, robotics, communications, speech, and social media. Particular attention is given to efficiency and reliability through sparse optimization, abstention, semi-supervised learning, fast text editing, and event-driven sensing. Finally, we consider privacy, security, causal accountability, and formal verification as essential complements to predictive performance. The synthesis identifies recurring trade-offs between accuracy, computational cost, interpretability, and robustness, and suggests that future intelligent systems should combine structured representations with adaptive learning and explicit guarantees concerning safety, privacy, and social impact.

original_abstract: State of the art visual relation detection methods have been relying on features extracted from RGB images including objects' 2D positions. In this paper, we argue that the 3D positions of objects in space can provide additional valuable information about object relations. This information helps not only to detect spatial relations, such as "standing behind", but also non-spatial relations, such as "holding". Since 3D information of a scene is not easily accessible, we propose incorporating a pre-trained RGB-to-Depth model within visual relation detection frameworks. We discuss different feature extraction strategies from depth maps and show their critical role in relation detection. Our experiments confirm that the performance of state-of-the-art visual relation detection approaches can significantly be improved by utilizing depth map information.

The results show that combining textual and relational information yields more coherent topic groups and more accurate recommendations than either source alone. The proposed framework offers a scalable basis for literature exploration, cross-disciplinary knowledge integration, and semi-automated scholarly review.

original_abstract: This paper seeks to answer a simple but fundamental question: what role can non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) play in massive multi-in multi-out (MIMO)? It is well established that power-domain NOMA schemes can outperform conventional orthogonal multiple access schemes in cellular networks. However, this fact does not imply that NOMA is the most efficient way to communicate in massive MIMO setups, where the base stations have many more antennas than there are users in the cell. These setups are becoming the norm in future networks and are usually studied by assuming spatial multiplexing of the users using linear multi-user beamforming. To answer the above-mentioned question, we analyze and compare the performance achieved by NOMA and multi-user beamforming in both non-line-of-sight and line-of-sight scenarios. We reveal that the latter scheme gives the highest average sum rate in massive MIMO setups. We also identify specific cases where NOMA is the better choice in massive MIMO and explain how NOMA plays an essential role in creating a hybrid of NOMA and multi-user beamforming that is shown to perform better than two standalone schemes do.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a unified perspective on graph- and network-based computation across mathematical, engineering, and data-driven applications. We examine how structural properties such as connectivity, symmetry, recurrence, and compositionality can be exploited to design scalable algorithms and reliable computational systems. We further consider emerging learning-based approaches in which structured representations improve efficiency and robustness, including recurrent models for quantitative magnetic resonance imaging, goal-directed exploration of Android applications, and steerable convolutional networks. Through these examples, we identify common trade-offs between exactness and efficiency, centralized specification and distributed execution, and invariance and expressiveness. The paper argues that explicit structural modeling is essential for controlling complexity while preserving the properties required by each application. We conclude by outlining research directions for combining formal guarantees, adaptive computation, and symmetry-aware learning in large-scale networked systems.

original_abstract: This paper proposes the first model-free Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework to synthesise policies for unknown, and continuous-state Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), such that a given linear temporal property is satisfied. We convert the given property into a Limit Deterministic Buchi Automaton (LDBA), namely a finite-state machine expressing the property. Exploiting the structure of the LDBA, we shape a synchronous reward function on-the-fly, so that an RL algorithm can synthesise a policy resulting in traces that probabilistically satisfy the linear temporal property. This probability (certificate) is also calculated in parallel with policy learning when the state space of the MDP is finite: as such, the RL algorithm produces a policy that is certified with respect to the property. Under the assumption of finite state space, theoretical guarantees are provided on the convergence of the RL algorithm to an optimal policy, maximising the above probability. We also show that our method produces ''best available'' control policies when the logical property cannot be satisfied. In the general case of a continuous state space, we propose a neural network architecture for RL and we empirically show that the algorithm finds satisfying policies, if there exist such policies. The performance of the proposed framework is evaluated via a set of numerical examples and benchmarks, where we observe an improvement of one order of magnitude in the number of iterations required for the policy synthesis, compared to existing approaches whenever available.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence and data-driven methods are increasingly being deployed across complex scientific, engineering, and social systems.
