In this paper we take on this major challenge and consider the problem of characterizing all testable graph properties in general planar graphs. #R##N#We consider the model in which a general planar graph can be accessed by the random neighbor oracle that allows access to any given vertex and access to a random neighbor of a given vertex. We show that, informally, a graph property $P$ is testable with one-sided error for general planar graphs if and only if testing $P$ can be reduced to testing for a finite family of finite forbidden subgraphs. While our presentation focuses on planar graphs, our approach extends easily to general minor-free graphs. #R##N#Our analysis of the necessary condition relies on a recent construction of canonical testers in the random neighbor oracle model that is applied here to the one-sided error model for testing in planar graphs. The sufficient condition in the characterization reduces the problem to the task of testing $H$-freeness in planar graphs, and is the main and most challenging technical contribution of the paper: we show that for planar graphs (with arbitrary degrees), the property of being $H$-free is testable with one-sided error for every finite graph $H$, in the random neighbor oracle model.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed across heterogeneous applications, platforms, and operating environments, yet existing benchmarks typically emphasize isolated kernels or a narrow class of models. This paper presents a comprehensive benchmark suite for evaluating AI systems from an end-to-end perspective. The suite covers representative workloads in computer vision, natural language processing, graph learning, signal processing, industrial diagnosis, multimedia analysis, privacy-preserving data management, and scientific and biological computing. These workloads capture diverse data modalities, model architectures, training and inference procedures, accuracy requirements, and resource demands, including sparsity, smoothness, noise, dynamic data, and large output spaces. We describe a unified methodology for workload specification, dataset preparation, execution, and measurement, enabling fair comparison across CPUs, GPUs, accelerators, and edge–cloud configurations. The benchmark reports both application quality and system performance, including throughput, latency, energy efficiency, memory use, scalability, and privacy-related costs. Experimental studies demonstrate that no single hardware or software design is optimal across the workload suite and that conclusions drawn from conventional microbenchmarks can be misleading. The proposed benchmark provides an open and extensible foundation for characterizing, optimizing, and co-designing future AI systems.

original_abstract: Neural Networks trained with gradient descent are known to be susceptible to catastrophic forgetting caused by parameter shift during the training process. In the context of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) this results in poor performance on heterogeneous datasets and on sub-tasks like rare phrase translation. On the other hand, non-parametric approaches are immune to forgetting, perfectly complementing the generalization ability of NMT. However, attempts to combine non-parametric or retrieval based approaches with NMT have only been successful on narrow domains, possibly due to over-reliance on sentence level retrieval. We propose a novel n-gram level retrieval approach that relies on local phrase level similarities, allowing us to retrieve neighbors that are useful for translation even when overall sentence similarity is low. We complement this with an expressive neural network, allowing our model to extract information from the noisy retrieved context. We evaluate our semi-parametric NMT approach on a heterogeneous dataset composed of WMT, IWSLT, JRC-Acquis and OpenSubtitles, and demonstrate gains on all 4 evaluation sets. The semi-parametric nature of our approach opens the door for non-parametric domain adaptation, demonstrating strong inference-time adaptation performance on new domains without the need for any parameter updates.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are increasingly applied across scientific, industrial, and societal domains, yet the rapid expansion of methods makes it difficult to compare approaches, assess their reliability, and select suitable techniques for a given problem. This paper presents a systematic, cross-domain analysis of contemporary AI methodologies, spanning supervised and unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, optimization, graph algorithms, natural language processing, computer vision, signal processing, causal inference, and distributed systems. We organize the literature according to learning setting, data structure, computational constraints, and evaluation objective, and examine recurring strategies for handling limited labels, domain shift, uncertainty, nonstationarity, communication costs, and model interpretability. Particular attention is given to reproducibility, benchmark design, robustness, scalability, and the distinction between predictive and causal performance. The review also identifies common opportunities for methodological transfer, such as geometric regularization, active learning, adaptive sampling, and error compensation. Our synthesis shows that progress increasingly depends not on isolated algorithmic innovations but on integrating domain knowledge, reliable evaluation, and efficient system design. We conclude with open challenges and recommendations for developing trustworthy, generalizable, and practically deployable AI systems.

original_abstract: Machine learning research has advanced in multiple aspects, including model structures and learning methods. The effort to automate such research, known as AutoML, has also made significant progress. However, this progress has largely focused on the architecture of neural networks, where it has relied on sophisticated expert-designed layers as building blocks---or similarly restrictive search spaces. Our goal is to show that AutoML can go further: it is possible today to automatically discover complete machine learning algorithms just using basic mathematical operations as building blocks. We demonstrate this by introducing a novel framework that significantly reduces human bias through a generic search space. Despite the vastness of this space, evolutionary search can still discover two-layer neural networks trained by backpropagation. These simple neural networks can then be surpassed by evolving directly on tasks of interest, e.g. CIFAR-10 variants, where modern techniques emerge in the top algorithms, such as bilinear interactions, normalized gradients, and weight averaging. Moreover, evolution adapts algorithms to different task types: e.g., dropout-like techniques appear when little data is available. We believe these preliminary successes in discovering machine learning algorithms from scratch indicate a promising new direction for the field.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a broad computational framework for analyzing and controlling complex systems characterized by heterogeneous data, structural constraints, uncertainty, and changing environments. We review and connect recent advances in machine learning, graph algorithms, optimization, formal verification, signal processing, robotics, language technologies, and networked systems. Particular attention is given to methods that combine data-driven inference with explicit structure, including graph-based representations, recurrent and convolutional models, kernel methods, adaptive sampling, decomposition techniques, and parameterized algorithms. We discuss how these approaches support perception, prediction, decision-making, anomaly detection, resource allocation, and system design across applications ranging from autonomous vehicles and cloud services to medical imaging, communication networks, biological analysis, and social choice. The comparison highlights recurring challenges: computational scalability, limited or noisy supervision, interpretability, robustness to distribution shift, and the need for guarantees on correctness or performance. We identify opportunities for integrating learning with optimization and formal reasoning, developing adaptive algorithms that exploit domain structure, and designing unified systems that remain efficient under resource and data constraints. The resulting perspective provides a foundation for future research on reliable, scalable, and interdisciplinary computational intelligence.

original_abstract: In person re-identification (Re-ID), supervised methods usually need a large amount of expensive label information, while unsupervised ones are still unable to deliver satisfactory identification performance. In this paper, we introduce a novel person Re-ID task called unsupervised cross-camera person Re-ID, which only needs the within-camera (intra-camera) label information but not cross-camera (inter-camera) labels which are more expensive to obtain. In real-world applications, the intra-camera label information can be easily captured by tracking algorithms or few manual annotations. In this situation, the main challenge becomes the distribution discrepancy across different camera views, caused by the various body pose, occlusion, image resolution, illumination conditions, and background noises in different cameras. To address this situation, we propose a novel Adversarial Camera Alignment Network (ACAN) for unsupervised cross-camera person Re-ID. It consists of the camera-alignment task and the supervised within-camera learning task. To achieve the camera alignment, we develop a Multi-Camera Adversarial Learning (MCAL) to map images of different cameras into a shared subspace. Particularly, we investigate two different schemes, including the existing GRL (i.e., gradient reversal layer) scheme and the proposed scheme called "other camera equiprobability" (OCE), to conduct the multi-camera adversarial task. Based on this shared subspace, we then leverage the within-camera labels to train the network. Extensive experiments on five large-scale datasets demonstrate the superiority of ACAN over multiple state-of-the-art unsupervised methods that take advantage of labeled source domains and generated images by GAN-based models. In particular, we verify that the proposed multi-camera adversarial task does contribute to the significant improvement.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is increasingly embedded in scientific, industrial, and safety-critical systems, yet progress is fragmented across application domains and methodological communities. This paper presents a systematic review of contemporary learning-based approaches, spanning supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, representation, and structured learning. We organize the literature according to the learning objective, data modality, model architecture, deployment setting, and evaluation criterion, and examine recurring challenges including distribution shift, limited or weakly labeled data, uncertainty quantification, adversarial manipulation, privacy, computational scalability, and interpretability. Across applications such as language, vision, healthcare, communications, transportation, energy, and networked systems, we identify common design patterns: exploiting structure in the data, incorporating domain knowledge, adapting models online, and combining learning with optimization or formal guarantees. We also compare strategies for improving robustness, efficiency, and transfer across environments, emphasizing the gap between benchmark performance and reliable deployment. The review highlights promising directions in self-supervision, multimodal learning, continual adaptation, safe exploration, and resource-aware inference. Finally, it proposes a practical evaluation framework that considers accuracy together with fairness, stability, security, computational cost, and reproducibility, providing guidance for developing dependable learning systems in complex real-world settings.

original_abstract: Visual navigation tasks in real-world environments often require both self-motion and place recognition feedback. While deep reinforcement learning has shown success in solving these perception and decision-making problems in an end-to-end manner, these algorithms require large amounts of experience to learn navigation policies from high-dimensional data, which is generally impractical for real robots due to sample complexity. In this paper, we address these problems with two main contributions. We first leverage place recognition and deep learning techniques combined with goal destination feedback to generate compact, bimodal image representations that can then be used to effectively learn control policies from a small amount of experience. Second, we present an interactive framework, CityLearn, that enables for the first time training and deployment of navigation algorithms across city-sized, realistic environments with extreme visual appearance changes. CityLearn features more than 10 benchmark datasets, often used in visual place recognition and autonomous driving research, including over 100 recorded traversals across 60 cities around the world. We evaluate our approach on two CityLearn environments, training our navigation policy on a single traversal. Results show our method can be over 2 orders of magnitude faster than when using raw images, and can also generalize across extreme visual changes including day to night and summer to winter transitions.
generated_abstract: We present a general framework for discovering and organizing scientific knowledge across heterogeneous research domains. The approach represents publications, authors, topics, methods, and citation relationships in a unified scholarly network, while combining textual features with structural and temporal information. To address the diversity of terminology and writing styles, we use contextual language representations together with graph-based propagation and attention mechanisms that identify the most informative neighboring documents. The framework supports several related tasks, including citation recommendation, topic classification, retrieval of technically similar work, and prediction of emerging connections between research areas. We evaluate it on a broad collection of publications spanning computer science, engineering, social science, mathematics, and biomedical research. Results show that incorporating citation structure substantially improves over text-only and conventional bibliometric baselines, particularly for interdisciplinary papers and sparse research communities. Qualitative analyses indicate that the model can recover meaningful methodological relationships even when papers use different vocabularies or address distinct applications. The proposed representation offers an interpretable basis for navigating large scholarly collections and may assist researchers, digital libraries, and research evaluators in identifying relevant knowledge and previously overlooked connections.

original_abstract: This paper proposes a framework which is able to generate a sequence of three-dimensional human dance poses for a given music. The proposed framework consists of three components: a music feature encoder, a pose generator, and a music genre classifier. We focus on integrating these components for generating a realistic 3D human dancing move from music, which can be applied to artificial agents and humanoid robots. The trained dance pose generator, which is a generative autoregressive model, is able to synthesize a dance sequence longer than 5,000 pose frames. Experimental results of generated dance sequences from various songs show how the proposed method generates human-like dancing move to a given music. In addition, a generated 3D dance sequence is applied to a humanoid robot, showing that the proposed framework can make a robot to dance just by listening to music.
generated_abstract: We present a multimodal framework for intelligent mobile robots operating in dynamic human environments. The system integrates visual perception, language understanding, sequential prediction, localization, navigation, and affect-aware interaction into a unified decision-making architecture. Human pose and gait are estimated from camera and wearable-sensor observations, while scene coordinates and graph representations support robust localization and modeling of relations among people, objects, and places. A recurrent generative module predicts the evolution of partially observed activities, and an entity-centered transformer tracks the state of relevant agents through procedural language and multimodal events. These representations are combined by a decision layer based on approximate Markov decision processes, allowing the robot to select safe, socially appropriate, and task-effective actions. The framework also incorporates redundancy-aware information retrieval and adaptive optimization to improve robustness under uncertain observations and changing environments. We evaluate the approach on simulated and physical-robot tasks involving navigation, human following, gesture and activity recognition, and cooperative game play. Results indicate improved localization accuracy, prediction quality, interaction success, and collision avoidance compared with independently trained perception and control pipelines. The study demonstrates that explicitly modeling temporal context, relational structure, and human affect is essential for dependable long-term human–robot interaction.

original_abstract: What is the current state-of-the-art for image restoration and enhancement applied to degraded images acquired under less than ideal circumstances? Can the application of such algorithms as a pre-processing step to improve image interpretability for manual analysis or automatic visual recognition to classify scene content? While there have been important advances in the area of computational photography to restore or enhance the visual quality of an image, the capabilities of such techniques have not always translated in a useful way to visual recognition tasks. Consequently, there is a pressing need for the development of algorithms that are designed for the joint problem of improving visual appearance and recognition, which will be an enabling factor for the deployment of visual recognition tools in many real-world scenarios. To address this, we introduce the UG^2 dataset as a large-scale benchmark composed of video imagery captured under challenging conditions, and two enhancement tasks designed to test algorithmic impact on visual quality and automatic object recognition. Furthermore, we propose a set of metrics to evaluate the joint improvement of such tasks as well as individual algorithmic advances, including a novel psychophysics-based evaluation regime for human assessment and a realistic set of quantitative measures for object recognition performance. We introduce six new algorithms for image restoration or enhancement, which were created as part of the IARPA sponsored UG^2 Challenge workshop held at CVPR 2018. Under the proposed evaluation regime, we present an in-depth analysis of these algorithms and a host of deep learning-based and classic baseline approaches. From the observed results, it is evident that we are in the early days of building a bridge between computational photography and visual recognition, leaving many opportunities for innovation in this area.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence and data-driven computation are increasingly deployed across scientific, engineering, and societal applications, from robotic manipulation and autonomous vehicles to wireless communication, medical diagnosis, education, and social media analysis. This paper surveys representative developments in learning, optimization, probabilistic modeling, simulation, and hardware-aware computing, with emphasis on the challenges that arise when methods move from controlled benchmarks to real-world environments. We organize existing approaches according to their data requirements, computational constraints, uncertainty models, and interaction with domain knowledge. Particular attention is given to transfer and continual learning, efficient inference, robustness to distribution shift and adversarial conditions, privacy and security, and the evaluation of systems in their intended operational context. We also discuss emerging directions, including structured and sparse neural architectures, neuromorphic and optical computing, topological and Koopman-based analysis, and human-centered quality assurance. Across domains, the literature indicates that accuracy alone is insufficient: dependable systems require interpretable representations, efficient resource use, explicit safety and security guarantees, and evaluation that includes users, infrastructure, and changing environments. We conclude with open research questions for building reusable, trustworthy, and scalable intelligent systems.

original_abstract: A classifier trained on a dataset seldom works on other datasets obtained under different conditions due to domain shift. This problem is commonly addressed by domain adaptation methods. In this work we introduce a novel deep learning framework which unifies different paradigms in unsupervised domain adaptation. Specifically, we propose domain alignment layers which implement feature whitening for the purpose of matching source and target feature distributions. Additionally, we leverage the unlabeled target data by proposing the Min-Entropy Consensus loss, which regularizes training while avoiding the adoption of many user-defined hyper-parameters. We report results on publicly available datasets, considering both digit classification and object recognition tasks. We show that, in most of our experiments, our approach improves upon previous methods, setting new state-of-the-art performances.
generated_abstract: We present a citation-aware framework for reconstructing the scientific content of a paper when its abstract is unavailable. The method represents cited publications using their titles, abstracts, methodological descriptions, and cross-disciplinary semantic relationships, then combines these signals to infer the missing paper’s research problem, technical contributions, and evaluation setting. Unlike approaches that rely solely on citation frequency or textual similarity, our framework distinguishes foundational theory, methodological precedents, application domains, and comparative baselines. A hierarchical encoder first identifies thematic clusters among cited works, while an attention-based generator integrates the most informative clusters into a concise abstract. We evaluate the approach on a collection of scientific articles with abstracts masked at test time, measuring lexical similarity, semantic agreement, factual consistency, and expert judgments of usefulness. Results show that citation structure provides substantial information about a paper’s scope, even when references span diverse fields such as machine learning, optimization, robotics, coding theory, networking, and computational science. Ablation studies demonstrate that combining citation context with abstract-level embeddings improves both factual precision and coverage over title-only and retrieval-based baselines. The proposed framework offers a practical tool for digital libraries, scholarly search, metadata recovery, and large-scale literature analysis.

original_abstract: Recent advancements in machine learning research, i.e., deep learning, introduced methods that excel conventional algorithms as well as humans in several complex tasks, ranging from detection of objects in images and speech recognition to playing difficult strategic games. However, the current methodology of machine learning research and consequently, implementations of the real-world applications of such algorithms, seems to have a recurring HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) issue. In this work, we elaborate on the algorithmic, economic and social reasons and consequences of this phenomenon. We present examples from current common practices of conducting machine learning research (e.g. avoidance of reporting negative results) and failure of generalization ability of the proposed algorithms and datasets in actual real-life usage. Furthermore, a potential future trajectory of machine learning research and development from the perspective of accountable, unbiased, ethical and privacy-aware algorithmic decision making is discussed. We would like to emphasize that with this discussion we neither claim to provide an exhaustive argumentation nor blame any specific institution or individual on the raised issues. This is simply a discussion put forth by us, insiders of the machine learning field, reflecting on us.
generated_abstract: Data science has emerged as an interdisciplinary field that combines statistical reasoning, machine learning, computational methods, and domain expertise to extract actionable knowledge from complex data. This paper examines the foundations, current practices, and future directions of data science across scientific, engineering, social, and industrial applications. We discuss the complete data lifecycle, including acquisition, storage, compression, integration, representation, modeling, evaluation, deployment, and communication. Particular attention is given to challenges arising from large-scale, dynamic, heterogeneous, and imperfect data, such as changing distributions, limited labels, out-of-domain cases, privacy risks, and the need for interpretable results. We review representative approaches for online learning, structured prediction, distributed optimization, graph and tensor analysis, neural modeling, and interactive analytics, emphasizing the trade-offs among accuracy, efficiency, robustness, and transparency. We also consider the human and organizational dimensions of the field, including domain collaboration, education, reproducibility, and responsible use. Finally, we propose a framework for organizing data science research and identify open problems concerning trustworthy automation, scalable infrastructure, explainability, and the translation of computational results into reliable decisions.

original_abstract: Recently, the problem of allocating one resource per agent with initial endowments (\emph{house markets}) has seen a renewed interest: indeed, while in the general domain Top Trading Cycle is known to be the only procedure guaranteeing Pareto-optimality, individual rationality, and strategy proofness, the situation differs in single-peaked domains. Bade (2019) presented the Crawler, an alternative procedure enjoying the same properties (with the additional advantage of being implementable in obviously dominant strategies); while Damamme et al. (2015) showed that allowing mutually beneficial swap-deals among the agents was already enough to guarantee Pareto-optimality. In this paper we significantly deepen our understanding of this decentralized procedures: we show in particular that the single-peaked domains happen to be ``maximal'' if one wishes to guarantee this convergence property. Interestingly, we also observe that the set of allocations reachable by swap-deals always contains the outcome of the Crawler. To further investigate how these different mechanisms compare, we pay special attention to the average and minimum rank of the resource obtained by the agents in the outcome allocation. We provide theoretical bounds on the loss potentially induced by these procedures with respect to these criteria, and complement these results with an extensive experimental study which shows how different variants of swap dynamics behave. In fact, even the simplest dynamics exhibit very good results, and it is possible to further guide the process towards our objectives, if one is ready to sacrifice a bit in terms of decentralization. On our way, we also show that a simple variant of the Crawler allows to check efficiently that an allocation is Pareto-optimal in single-peaked domains.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a unified perspective on the design of trustworthy, adaptive intelligent systems operating in complex real-world environments. We identify key requirements that extend beyond predictive accuracy, including scalability, continual learning, privacy, security, formal assurance, interpretability, and effective interaction with human users. The proposed framework organizes these requirements across the system lifecycle, from data acquisition and representation to learning, decision making, deployment, and runtime monitoring. It combines data-driven methods with symbolic knowledge, optimization, resource-aware decision making, and certified safeguards, allowing autonomous components to adapt while remaining within specified behavioral and safety constraints. Particular attention is given to heterogeneous and uncertain data, long-term task sequences, language and domain variation, and the protection of sensitive information. We further discuss how modular architectures, compositional reasoning, and runtime assurance can support the certification of systems whose behavior cannot be completely characterized at design time. The framework is illustrated through representative applications in cyber-physical control, smart infrastructure, software development, language technologies, and biomedical analysis. Our analysis highlights open challenges in evaluating reliability, coordinating interacting agents, and reconciling adaptation with accountability, and provides directions for developing intelligent systems that are both capable and dependable.

original_abstract: In this paper, we address the open question: "What do adversarially robust models look at?" Recently, it has been reported in many works that there exists the trade-off between standard accuracy and adversarial robustness. According to prior works, this trade-off is rooted in the fact that adversarially robust and standard accurate models might depend on very different sets of features. However, it has not been well studied what kind of difference actually exists. In this paper, we analyze this difference through various experiments visually and quantitatively. Experimental results show that adversarially robust models look at things at a larger scale than standard models and pay less attention to fine textures. Furthermore, although it has been claimed that adversarially robust features are not compatible with standard accuracy, there is even a positive effect by using them as pre-trained models particularly in low resolution datasets.
generated_abstract: This paper examines how modern computational methods are being developed and applied across a broad range of scientific and engineering domains. We survey approaches based on machine learning, deep neural networks, probabilistic modeling, graph algorithms, optimization, formal logic, and information theory, emphasizing the common principles that connect seemingly different applications. These methods support tasks including perception, prediction, language processing, biological and medical analysis, network control, robotics, communications, cybersecurity, and large-scale data management. Particular attention is given to representation learning, transfer across domains, uncertainty quantification, efficient inference, and the trade-offs among accuracy, computational cost, privacy, and reliability. We also discuss the importance of incorporating structure and prior knowledge, whether expressed through physical models, scene geometry, logical constraints, network topology, or domain-specific supervision. Across applications, performance depends not only on model capacity but also on data quality, validation design, robustness to distribution shifts, and the ability to operate under limited resources. The paper identifies recurring methodological challenges and outlines directions for building computational systems that are more interpretable, adaptable, efficient, and dependable in real-world settings.

original_abstract: Deep learning natural language processing models often use vector word embeddings, such as word2vec or GloVe, to represent words. A discrete sequence of words can be much more easily integrated with downstream neural layers if it is represented as a sequence of continuous vectors. Also, semantic relationships between words, learned from a text corpus, can be encoded in the relative configurations of the embedding vectors. However, storing and accessing embedding vectors for all words in a dictionary requires large amount of space, and may stain systems with limited GPU memory. Here, we used approaches inspired by quantum computing to propose two related methods, {\em word2ket} and {\em word2ketXS}, for storing word embedding matrix during training and inference in a highly efficient way. Our approach achieves a hundred-fold or more reduction in the space required to store the embeddings with almost no relative drop in accuracy in practical natural language processing tasks.
generated_abstract: We present a framework for discovering and organizing heterogeneous scientific literature through the joint analysis of article text, citation links, and metadata. The approach is motivated by the difficulty of searching across disciplinary boundaries, where papers addressing related methodological ideas may use substantially different terminology. We construct document representations from titles, abstracts, and citation contexts, combine these representations with the structure of the citation network, and learn a unified low-dimensional embedding of the scholarly collection. The framework supports semantic retrieval, clustering, citation recommendation, and exploration of emerging connections between fields. To assess its utility, we evaluate it on a diverse corpus spanning machine learning, network science, information theory, computational mathematics, social science, and the humanities. Results show that incorporating citation structure improves retrieval of conceptually related papers over text-only and citation-only baselines, while citation-context modeling reduces the influence of highly cited but weakly related publications. Qualitative analyses further demonstrate that the method identifies methodological connections that are not apparent from keywords alone. The proposed framework offers a scalable basis for cross-disciplinary literature analysis and more transparent navigation of large scholarly collections.

original_abstract: Time series forecasting is one of the challenging problems for humankind. The traditional forecasting methods using mean regression models have severe shortcomings in reflecting real-world fluctuations. While new probabilistic methods rush to rescue, they fight with technical difficulties like quantile crossing or selecting a prior distribution. To meld the different strengths of these fields while avoiding their weaknesses, as well as, to push the boundary of the state-of-the-art, we introduce ForGAN - one step ahead probabilistic forecasting with generative adversarial networks. ForGAN utilizes the power of the conditional generative adversarial network to learn the data generating distribution and compute probabilistic forecasts from it. We argue how to evaluate ForGAN in opposition to regression methods. To investigate probabilistic forecasting of ForGAN, we create a new dataset and demonstrate our method abilities on it. This dataset will be made publicly available for comparison. Furthermore, we test ForGAN on two publicly available datasets, namely Mackey-Glass dataset and Internet traffic dataset (A5M), where the impressive performance of ForGAN demonstrate its high capability in forecasting future values.
generated_abstract: We present a general framework for learning representations of scientific publications from heterogeneous bibliographic information. The method combines textual content, citation links, authorship and venue metadata, and semantic relationships between cited works to model the structure of the scientific literature. Unlike approaches that rely solely on citation counts or document similarity, our framework captures both the topical and relational context in which publications are used. We formulate citation recommendation and related-paper retrieval as representation-learning tasks and investigate the effects of incorporating graph structure, textual semantics, and heterogeneous side information. Experiments on a broad collection of publications spanning computer science, engineering, mathematics, social science, and the humanities show that integrating citation and content signals consistently improves retrieval and link-prediction performance over text-only and graph-only baselines. Qualitative analyses further indicate that the learned representations identify meaningful cross-disciplinary connections and distinguish papers with similar topics but different scientific roles. The results demonstrate the value of jointly modeling scholarly text and citation networks for navigating large research collections, supporting literature discovery, and revealing emerging relationships among scientific contributions.

original_abstract: When one wants to train a neural network to perform semantic segmentation, creating pixel-level annotations for each of the images in the database is a tedious task. If he works with aerial or satellite images, which are usually very large, it is even worse. With that in mind, we investigate how to use image-level annotations in order to perform semantic segmentation. Image-level annotations are much less expensive to acquire than pixel-level annotations, but we lose a lot of information for the training of the model. From the annotations of the images, the model must find by itself how to classify the different regions of the image. In this work, we use the method proposed by Anh and Kwak [1] to produce pixel-level annotation from image level annotation. We compare the overall quality of our generated dataset with the original dataset. In addition, we propose an adaptation of the AffinityNet that allows us to directly perform a semantic segmentation. Our results show that the generated labels lead to the same performances for the training of several segmentation networks. Also, the quality of semantic segmentation performed directly by the AffinityNet and the Random Walk is close to the one of the best fully-supervised approaches.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly developing as an interdisciplinary engineering and scientific discipline, combining statistical learning, optimization, formal methods, control, and domain-specific knowledge. This paper surveys emerging directions in intelligent systems and examines how these approaches address complex problems in science, industry, and society. We discuss data-driven models for physical processes, biological network reconstruction, medical genomics, image classification, navigation, and cooperative robotics, together with optimization methods for energy systems and virtualized datacenters. We also consider the integration of learning with structured representations, including geometric, logical, relational, and probabilistic frameworks, and highlight applications in databases and information retrieval. Because intelligent systems increasingly operate in critical and distributed infrastructures, the paper reviews privacy-preserving computation, hardware security, cloud vulnerabilities, and adversarial robustness in machine-learning-based malware detection. Across these areas, common challenges emerge: uncertainty, sparse and heterogeneous data, scalability, interpretability, coordination, and reliable transfer from laboratory settings to real environments. We argue that progress will depend on principled combinations of learning and reasoning, adaptive human–machine collaboration, secure system design, and evaluation practices that reflect both technical performance and societal consequences.

original_abstract: The advice model of online computation captures the setting in which the online algorithm is given some partial information concerning the request sequence. This paradigm allows to establish tradeoffs between the amount of this additional information and the performance of the online algorithm. However, unlike real life in which advice is a recommendation that we can chose to follow or to ignore based on trustworthiness, in the current advice model, the online algorithm treats it as infallible. This means that if the advice is corrupt or, worse, if it comes from a malicious source, the algorithm may perform poorly. In this work, we study online computation in a setting in which the advice is provided by an untrusted source. Our objective is to quantify the impact of untrusted advice so as to design and analyze online algorithms that are resilient and perform well even when the advice is generated in a malicious, adversarial manner. To this end, we focus on well-studied online problems such as ski rental, online bidding, bin packing, and list update. For ski-rental and online bidding, we show how to obtain algorithms that are Pareto-optimal with respect to the competitive ratios achieved; this improves upon the framework of Purohit et al. [NeurIPS 2018] in which Pareto-optimality is not necessarily guaranteed. For bin packing and list update, we give online algorithms with worst-case tradeoffs in their competitiveness, depending on whether the advice is trusted or not; this is motivated by work of Lykouris and Vassilvitskii [ICML 2018] on the paging problem, but in which the competitiveness depends on the reliability of the advice.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a multidisciplinary perspective on the design of trustworthy, adaptive, and resource-efficient intelligent systems operating at the network edge. We examine how emerging applications combine machine learning, wireless communication, coding theory, robotics, and network security, while introducing new requirements for reliability, privacy, and real-time operation. We first review challenges in extracting reliable information from unmoderated online content and in protecting network infrastructure against spoofing and other attacks. We then discuss communication mechanisms that improve coexistence and interference management in dynamic spectrum environments, together with coding techniques that support robust transmission over packet networks. The role of embodied intelligence is considered through soft robotic systems, whose compliant structures enable safe interaction in uncertain and congested environments. Finally, we analyze systems techniques for deploying deep vision on mobile devices, emphasizing temporal reuse and energy-aware inference. Across these domains, we identify common principles, including adaptation to changing conditions, explicit management of uncertainty, and coordination between algorithms and hardware. We conclude by outlining open research directions for building scalable intelligent systems that are efficient, secure, and dependable in real-world settings.

original_abstract: The authors present a visual instrument developed as part of the creation of the artwork Learning to See. The artwork explores bias in artificial neural networks and provides mechanisms for the manipulation of specifically trained-for real-world representations. The exploration of these representations acts as a metaphor for the process of developing a visual understanding and/or visual vocabulary of the world. These representations can be explored and manipulated in real time, and have been produced in such a way so as to reflect specific creative perspectives that call into question the relationship between how both artificial neural networks and humans may construct meaning.
generated_abstract: Modern intelligent systems must acquire information selectively while balancing accuracy, computational cost, and security. This paper presents a general framework for adaptive information acquisition in which a system actively chooses observations, labels, or actions according to their expected utility and potential information leakage. The framework combines probabilistic belief updates with multi-objective optimization, allowing users to trade predictive performance against sensing, annotation, and privacy costs. We develop an anytime coordination procedure that incrementally constructs a set of solutions that are optimal for different objective preferences, and we provide bounds on the quality of intermediate solutions. To improve scalability, model adaptation and configuration are driven by active selection of the most informative data, while evolutionary search is used when the underlying model contains interacting hyperparameters. We further describe how leakage-aware constraints can protect sensitive attributes and how the framework supports authentication and other human-centered sensing tasks. Experiments across visual terrain classification, deep-model adaptation, software artifact analysis, multi-agent decision making, and physiological authentication demonstrate that the proposed approach reaches target performance with fewer observations and lower computational effort than conventional fixed-model or single-objective methods, while maintaining explicit control over privacy risk.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose a communication-efficient decentralized machine learning (ML) algorithm, coined quantized group ADMM (Q-GADMM). Every worker in Q-GADMM communicates only with two neighbors, and updates its model via the alternating direct method of multiplier (ADMM), thereby ensuring fast convergence while reducing the number of communication rounds. Furthermore, each worker quantizes its model updates before transmissions, thereby decreasing the communication payload sizes. We prove that Q-GADMM converges for convex loss functions, and numerically show that Q-GADMM yields 7x less communication cost while achieving almost the same accuracy and convergence speed compared to a baseline without quantization, group ADMM (GADMM).
generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for discovering and ranking scientific publications from heterogeneous scholarly information. The proposed system combines textual representations of titles, abstracts, and key terms with citation links, venue metadata, usage indicators, and author or topic relationships. A learning-to-rank component then estimates the relevance of candidate papers for a query, while an adaptive aggregation scheme balances content similarity, citation evidence, recency, and user behavior. The framework is designed to remain effective when abstracts are incomplete, terminology is domain-specific, or citation data are sparse. The method improves retrieval precision and ranking quality, particularly for interdisciplinary queries and less-established publications, while providing interpretable evidence for each recommendation. These results demonstrate that combining semantic and network information offers a practical basis for more accurate, diverse, and transparent scientific literature search.

original_abstract: Counting people or objects with significantly varying scales and densities has attracted much interest from the research community and yet it remains an open problem. In this paper, we propose a simple but an efficient and effective network, named DENet, which is composed of two components, i.e., a detection network (DNet) and an encoder-decoder estimation network (ENet). We first run DNet on an input image to detect and count individuals who can be segmented clearly. Then, ENet is utilized to estimate the density maps of the remaining areas, where the numbers of individuals cannot be detected. We propose a modified Xception as an encoder for feature extraction and a combination of dilated convolution and transposed convolution as a decoder. In the ShanghaiTech Part A, UCF and WorldExpo'10 datasets, our DENet achieves lower Mean Absolute Error (MAE) than those of the state-of-the-art methods.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning are increasingly being applied to complex problems involving perception, decision-making, optimization, control, and scientific discovery. This paper presents a cross-disciplinary review of recent approaches that combine learning with structured representations, explicit communication, probabilistic reasoning, and domain knowledge. We examine developments in image and speech understanding, scene and place representation, user profiling, medical image segmentation, metric learning, and adversarial robustness. We also consider AI-enabled coordination and planning in robotic swarms, agile project management, mixed-criticality scheduling, electric-vehicle grid services, distributed transaction systems, and network-coded communication. Further applications include crowd evacuation modeling, quantum-system control, compressive imaging, processing-in-storage architectures, materials discovery, and integration of single-cell transcriptomic data. Across these areas, the reviewed studies demonstrate that performance improves when models exploit task structure, uncertainty, temporal consistency, or iterative interaction with their environment. The paper identifies common challenges, including limited and heterogeneous data, distribution shift, computational cost, interpretability, safety, and the need for formal guarantees. It concludes by outlining opportunities for integrated, adaptive, and trustworthy AI systems that unite statistical learning with symbolic and physical knowledge.

original_abstract: In the last decade, numerous supervised deep learning approaches requiring large amounts of labeled data have been proposed for visual-inertial odometry (VIO) and depth map estimation. To overcome the data limitation, self-supervised learning has emerged as a promising alternative, exploiting constraints such as geometric and photometric consistency in the scene. In this study, we introduce a novel self-supervised deep learning-based VIO and depth map recovery approach (SelfVIO) using adversarial training and self-adaptive visual-inertial sensor fusion. SelfVIO learns to jointly estimate 6 degrees-of-freedom (6-DoF) ego-motion and a depth map of the scene from unlabeled monocular RGB image sequences and inertial measurement unit (IMU) readings. The proposed approach is able to perform VIO without the need for IMU intrinsic parameters and/or the extrinsic calibration between the IMU and the camera. estimation and single-view depth recovery network. We provide comprehensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations of the proposed framework comparing its performance with state-of-the-art VIO, VO, and visual simultaneous localization and mapping (VSLAM) approaches on the KITTI, EuRoC and Cityscapes datasets. Detailed comparisons prove that SelfVIO outperforms state-of-the-art VIO approaches in terms of pose estimation and depth recovery, making it a promising approach among existing methods in the literature.
generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for discovering, organizing, and exploiting knowledge from heterogeneous scholarly and technical data. The framework combines representation learning, probabilistic modeling, graph-based inference, optimization, and domain-specific constraints to support prediction, recommendation, classification, and decision making across diverse applications. It integrates textual, visual, temporal, relational, and sensor-derived information, while allowing prior knowledge and uncertainty to be incorporated explicitly. To improve reliability, we investigate generalization, interpretability, fairness, privacy, and robustness, including methods for identifying influential features, critical computational paths, and meaningful latent structures. The framework also supports active data acquisition and adaptive resource allocation, reducing annotation and computational costs in large-scale settings. We evaluate the resulting methods on benchmarks spanning communication networks, intelligent transportation, healthcare, education, robotics, computer vision, and energy systems. Across these tasks, the proposed approach consistently improves predictive accuracy, efficiency, or decision quality compared with conventional baselines, while retaining practical scalability. The results demonstrate that combining structured domain knowledge with modern learning algorithms can provide accurate, explainable, and adaptable solutions for complex real-world systems.

original_abstract: Pre-trained language models have been dominating the field of natural language processing in recent years, and have led to significant performance gains for various complex natural language tasks. One of the most prominent pre-trained language models is BERT (Bi-directional Encoders for Transformers), which was released as an English as well as a multilingual version. Although multilingual BERT performs well on many tasks, recent studies showed that BERT models trained on a single language significantly outperform the multilingual results. Training a Dutch BERT model thus has a lot of potential for a wide range of Dutch NLP tasks. While previous approaches have used earlier implementations of BERT to train their Dutch BERT, we used RoBERTa, a robustly optimized BERT approach, to train a Dutch language model called RobBERT. We show that RobBERT improves state of the art results in Dutch-specific language tasks, and also outperforms other existing Dutch BERT-based models in sentiment analysis. These results indicate that RobBERT is a powerful pre-trained model for fine-tuning for a large variety of Dutch language tasks. We publicly release this pre-trained model in hope of supporting further downstream Dutch NLP applications.
generated_abstract: Modern intelligent systems must balance accuracy with computational cost, communication overhead, privacy, reliability, and adaptability. This paper presents a unified resource-aware perspective on the design and evaluation of learning and algorithmic systems across centralized, distributed, and embedded environments. We organize existing approaches according to the resources they consume, including computation, memory, energy, bandwidth, data, and human supervision, and examine how these resources affect performance and scalability. The framework encompasses optimization methods, representation learning, multimodal sensing, approximate computation, privacy-preserving and federated learning, robust inference, and specialized hardware. We further discuss mechanisms for reducing resource demands, such as adaptive model complexity, dimensionality reduction, data and feature selection, augmentation, hierarchical communication, and fault-tolerant architectures. Particular attention is given to the trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, security, and generalization, as well as to methods for measuring these quantities consistently. Finally, we identify open challenges in reproducible benchmarking, online adaptation, cross-environment transfer, and deployment under strict resource constraints. The resulting perspective provides practical guidance for selecting algorithms and designing systems that remain effective when data, energy, computation, or communication are limited.

original_abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has seen an explosion of research in the past few years. A variety of methods have been proposed to perform NAS, including reinforcement learning, Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian process model, evolutionary search, and gradient descent. In this work, we design a NAS algorithm that performs Bayesian optimization using a neural network model. #R##N#We develop a path-based encoding scheme to featurize the neural architectures that are used to train the neural network model. This strategy is particularly effective for encoding architectures in cell-based search spaces. After training on just 200 random neural architectures, we are able to predict the validation accuracy of a new architecture to within one percent of its true accuracy on average, for popular search spaces. This may be of independent interest beyond Bayesian neural architecture search. #R##N#We test our algorithm on the NASBench (Ying et al. 2019) and DARTS (Liu et al. 2018) search spaces, and we show that our algorithm outperforms other NAS methods including evolutionary search, reinforcement learning, AlphaX, ASHA, and DARTS. Our algorithm is over 100x more efficient than random search, and 3.8x more efficient than the next-best algorithm on the NASBench dataset. As there have been problems with fair and reproducible experimental evauations in the field of NAS, we adhere to the recent NAS research checklist (Lindauer and Hutter 2019) to facilitate NAS research. In particular, our implementation has been made publicly available, including all details needed to fully reproduce our results.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence and machine learning now underpin applications ranging from scientific discovery and medical diagnosis to autonomous systems, communication networks, cybersecurity, and social interaction.
