We organize existing work into major themes, including deep and recurrent architectures, generative and adversarial models, attention and multimodal fusion, reinforcement and online learning, optimization, probabilistic modeling, and formal reasoning. We then examine their use in language and speech processing, computer vision and radiology, robotics, sensor and energy systems, wireless and software-defined networks, storage and coding, and scientific data analysis. Particular attention is given to interpretability, privacy and security, data quality, computational efficiency, resource constraints, and the reliability of learned decisions. Across these domains, we identify recurring trade-offs between accuracy, transparency, scalability, and robustness. The review concludes by outlining open challenges in combining symbolic and statistical approaches, learning from limited or noisy data, supporting human collaboration, and translating experimental results into dependable real-world systems.

original_abstract: Building robust and real-time classifiers with diverse datasets are one of the most significant challenges to deep learning researchers. It is because there is a considerable gap between a model built with training (seen) data and real (unseen) data in applications. Recent works including Zero-Shot Learning (ZSL), have attempted to deal with this problem of overcoming the apparent gap through transfer learning. In this paper, we propose a novel model, called Class Representative Learning Model (CRL), that can be especially effective in image classification influenced by ZSL. In the CRL model, first, the learning step is to build class representatives to represent classes in datasets by aggregating prominent features extracted from a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Second, the inferencing step in CRL is to match between the class representatives and new data. The proposed CRL model demonstrated superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art research in ZSL and mobile deep learning. The proposed CRL model has been implemented and evaluated in a parallel environment, using Apache Spark, for both distributed learning and recognition. An extensive experimental study on the benchmark datasets, ImageNet-1K, CalTech-101, CalTech-256, CIFAR-100, shows that CRL can build a class distribution model with drastic improvement in learning and recognition performance without sacrificing accuracy compared to the state-of-the-art performances in image classification.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being developed as an interdisciplinary field, combining statistical learning, symbolic reasoning, optimization, control, communication, and human-centered interaction. This paper reviews recent advances across these areas and examines how common computational principles support applications ranging from computer vision, language understanding, robotics, and autonomous systems to wireless networks, medical imaging, computational biology, and software engineering. We organize existing methods according to their treatment of data, knowledge, uncertainty, structure, and feedback, highlighting connections between apparently distinct approaches such as neural networks, probabilistic logic, tensor representations, game-theoretic optimization, and formal verification. Particular attention is given to the trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, interpretability, privacy, robustness, and safety in real-world deployments. We also discuss emerging directions, including hybrid model-based and model-free intelligence, self-supervised and weakly supervised learning, distributed computation, privacy-preserving data use, and learning-based control with stability guarantees. The review identifies persistent challenges in generalization, evaluation, reproducibility, human oversight, and responsible deployment, and argues that progress toward broadly capable intelligent systems will depend on integrating complementary methods rather than pursuing isolated improvements within individual application domains.

original_abstract: Inductive representation learning on temporal graphs is an important step toward salable machine learning on real-world dynamic networks. The evolving nature of temporal dynamic graphs requires handling new nodes as well as capturing temporal patterns. The node embeddings, which are now functions of time, should represent both the static node features and the evolving topological structures. Moreover, node and topological features can be temporal as well, whose patterns the node embeddings should also capture. We propose the temporal graph attention (TGAT) layer to efficiently aggregate temporal-topological neighborhood features as well as to learn the time-feature interactions. For TGAT, we use the self-attention mechanism as building block and develop a novel functional time encoding technique based on the classical Bochner's theorem from harmonic analysis. By stacking TGAT layers, the network recognizes the node embeddings as functions of time and is able to inductively infer embeddings for both new and observed nodes as the graph evolves. The proposed approach handles both node classification and link prediction task, and can be naturally extended to include the temporal edge features. We evaluate our method with transductive and inductive tasks under temporal settings with two benchmark and one industrial dataset. Our TGAT model compares favorably to state-of-the-art baselines as well as the previous temporal graph embedding approaches.
generated_abstract: We present a general framework for designing reliable learning and decision-making systems under uncertainty, incomplete observations, and changing operating conditions. The framework combines representation learning, probabilistic modeling, optimization, and domain-specific structural constraints to improve both predictive performance and interpretability. It supports heterogeneous data sources, including time series, images, event logs, network measurements, and clinical records, and can be adapted to supervised, unsupervised, and sequential decision problems. A central component is an uncertainty-aware learning strategy that distinguishes invariant information from context-dependent variation and uses this distinction for robust inference, resource allocation, and anomaly detection. We further introduce mechanisms for efficient computation, including sparse representations, approximate inference, adaptive sampling, and scalable deep architectures. Experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets covering signal recovery, visual recognition, tracking, medical prognosis, communication networks, and emergency monitoring demonstrate consistent improvements over conventional statistical, optimization-based, and deep-learning baselines. The results show that incorporating structural knowledge and explicit uncertainty estimates can increase accuracy, reduce computational and communication costs, and provide more dependable decisions when data distributions, sensing conditions, or system components change.

original_abstract: Lexical relations describe how concepts are semantically related, in the form of relation triples. The accurate prediction of lexical relations between concepts is challenging, due to the sparsity of patterns indicating the existence of such relations. We propose the Knowledge-Enriched Meta-Learning (KEML) framework to address the task of lexical relation classification. In KEML, the LKB-BERT (Lexical Knowledge Base-BERT) model is presented to learn concept representations from massive text corpora, with rich lexical knowledge injected by distant supervision. A probabilistic distribution of auxiliary tasks is defined to increase the model's ability to recognize different types of lexical relations. We further combine a meta-learning process over the auxiliary task distribution and supervised learning to train the neural lexical relation classifier. Experiments over multiple datasets show that KEML outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for discovering, organizing, and analyzing heterogeneous scientific knowledge from scholarly publications. The framework combines knowledge-graph representations with neural language models, semantic relation extraction, topic-hierarchy summarization, and evidence-aware information retrieval. Publications are represented as interconnected entities involving authors, concepts, methods, datasets, results, and citation relationships, while provenance annotations preserve the sources and transformations supporting each inferred relation. To accommodate the diversity of scientific domains, the system integrates supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised learning, including representation learning, clustering, classification, and graph-based inference. An incremental processing architecture enables new documents and corrections to be incorporated without reconstructing the entire graph, and uncertainty estimates distinguish extracted evidence from inferred knowledge. We evaluate the framework on a large, multidisciplinary collection of research articles using tasks including topic assignment, related-work discovery, citation recommendation, and multi-document summarization. Results show that combining textual, structural, and provenance information improves retrieval and classification over text-only baselines, while substantially reducing the effort required to navigate unfamiliar research areas. The framework provides a practical foundation for reproducible literature analysis, scholarly search, and machine-assisted knowledge synthesis.

original_abstract: This paper proposes a new method for live free-viewpoint human performance capture with dynamic details (e.g., cloth wrinkles) using a single RGBD camera. Our main contributions are: (i) a multi-layer representation of garments and body, and (ii) a physics-based performance capture procedure. We first digitize the performer using multi-layer surface representation, which includes the undressed body surface and separate clothing meshes. For performance capture, we perform skeleton tracking, cloth simulation, and iterative depth fitting sequentially for the incoming frame. By incorporating cloth simulation into the performance capture pipeline, we can simulate plausible cloth dynamics and cloth-body interactions even in the occluded regions, which was not possible in previous capture methods. Moreover, by formulating depth fitting as a physical process, our system produces cloth tracking results consistent with the depth observation while still maintaining physical constraints. Results and evaluations show the effectiveness of our method. Our method also enables new types of applications such as cloth retargeting, free-viewpoint video rendering and animations.
generated_abstract: Scientific knowledge is distributed across specialized publications, expressed in incompatible terminology, and difficult to compare or reuse systematically. We present a framework for constructing an interoperable knowledge graph from heterogeneous scientific literature. The framework represents findings as atomic, independently interpretable claims and links them to methods, data, domains, authors, and supporting or conflicting evidence. A combination of linguistic normalization, machine-assisted claim extraction, semantic similarity, and human validation is used to transform papers from fields including machine learning, communications, robotics, medicine, and remote sensing into a common representation. The resulting graph supports semantic search, aggregation of evidence, identification of methodological relationships, and detection of possible inconsistencies. We further describe procedures for assessing claim reliability, tracing conclusions to their original sources, and preserving uncertainty when evidence is incomplete or contradictory. An exploratory evaluation on a diverse collection of publications shows that the representation can capture both technical results and contextual information while remaining understandable to non-specialists. The results suggest that structured claim networks can complement conventional citation indexes and provide a practical foundation for automated literature review, fact checking, hypothesis discovery, and collaborative scientific communication.

original_abstract: Relational reasoning - the ability to model interactions and relations between objects - is valuable for robust multi-object tracking and pivotal for trajectory prediction. In this paper, we propose MOHART, a class-agnostic, end-to-end multi-object tracking and trajectory prediction algorithm, which explicitly accounts for permutation invariance in its relational reasoning. We explore a number of permutation invariant architectures and show that multi-headed self-attention outperforms the provided baselines and better accounts for complex physical interactions in a challenging toy experiment. We show on three real-world tracking datasets that adding relational reasoning capabilities in this way increases the tracking and trajectory prediction performance, particularly in the presence of ego-motion, occlusions, crowded scenes, and faulty sensor inputs. To the best of our knowledge, MOHART is the first fully end-to-end multi-object tracking from vision approach applied to real-world data reported in the literature.
generated_abstract: Complex networks arise in communication systems, healthcare, transportation, supply chains, social media, scientific collaboration, and many other domains. Their analysis increasingly combines graph-theoretic models, statistical inference, machine learning, optimization, and simulation, yet methods are often developed and evaluated in isolation. This paper presents an interdisciplinary framework for studying large, heterogeneous networks from data to decision making. We review approaches for network generation and characterization, including higher-order models, community structure, core–periphery organization, propagation effects, and temporal availability. We then examine learning-based techniques for representation, classification, prediction, and anomaly or attack detection, together with optimization methods for resource allocation, routing, reliability, and resilience. Particular attention is given to practical constraints such as incomplete and noisy observations, scalability, uncertainty, privacy, and latency. Through examples drawn from wireless communications, medical referrals, online platforms, document collections, and infrastructure systems, we show how network structure can guide algorithm design and how learned representations can improve network control. The study identifies common methodological principles, discusses limitations of current benchmarks and evaluation measures, and outlines opportunities for integrating graph learning, causal analysis, and robust optimization in future networked systems.

original_abstract: Concolic testing is a test generation technique which works effectively by integrating random testing generation and symbolic execution. Existing concolic testing engines focus on numeric programs. Heap-manipulating programs make extensive use of complex heap objects like trees and lists. Testing such programs is challenging due to multiple reasons. Firstly, test inputs for such program are required to satisfy non-trivial constraints which must be specified precisely. Secondly, precisely encoding and solving path conditions in such programs are challenging and often expensive. In this work, we propose the first concolic testing engine called CSF for heap-manipulating programs based on separation logic. CSF effectively combines specification-based testing and concolic execution for test input generation. It is evaluated on a set of challenging heap-manipulating programs. The results show that CSF generates valid test inputs with high coverage efficiently. Furthermore, we show that CSF can be potentially used in combination with precondition inference tools to reduce the user effort.
generated_abstract: We present a general framework for learning and decision making from complex, partially observed data streams. The framework combines multiscale representations for capturing local and nonlocal structure, attention-based recurrent models for forecasting evolving scenes, and compact probabilistic sketches for estimating high-dimensional connectivity statistics under strict memory and latency constraints. To support reliable decisions when observations are incomplete, we develop a queue-aware sampling strategy that prioritizes information according to current system state and establish performance guarantees using large-deviation analysis. We further introduce an algebraic perspective on model degeneracy, characterizing unstable configurations through one-parameter transformations and providing practical criteria for detecting them without explicitly computing all invariants. The resulting methodology is evaluated on three representative tasks: binary image segmentation, distorted scene-text recognition, and real-time network monitoring. Across these settings, the proposed representations improve predictive accuracy, reduce computational and memory requirements, and remain robust to geometric distortion, missing observations, and rapidly changing inputs. The results demonstrate that combining structural priors, adaptive attention, and principled uncertainty analysis offers a practical route toward efficient inference in dynamic environments.

original_abstract: Recent research advances in Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing have introduced novel tasks that are paving the way for solving AI-complete problems. One of those tasks is called Visual Question Answering (VQA). A VQA system must take an image and a free-form, open-ended natural language question about the image, and produce a natural language answer as the output. Such a task has drawn great attention from the scientific community, which generated a plethora of approaches that aim to improve the VQA predictive accuracy. Most of them comprise three major components: (i) independent representation learning of images and questions; (ii) feature fusion so the model can use information from both sources to answer visual questions; and (iii) the generation of the correct answer in natural language. With so many approaches being recently introduced, it became unclear the real contribution of each component for the ultimate performance of the model. The main goal of this paper is to provide a comprehensive analysis regarding the impact of each component in VQA models. Our extensive set of experiments cover both visual and textual elements, as well as the combination of these representations in form of fusion and attention mechanisms. Our major contribution is to identify core components for training VQA models so as to maximize their predictive performance.
generated_abstract: This paper surveys recent advances in computational methods for learning, optimization, networking, security, and data-intensive applications. We organize the literature around several recurring challenges: learning useful representations from limited or distorted data, designing efficient and scalable architectures, achieving robustness under adversarial or changing conditions, and providing interpretable decisions. We review developments in deep representation learning, self-supervised and adversarial training, neural architecture design, hashing, visual recognition, and structured prediction, alongside theoretical progress in stochastic approximation, evolutionary optimization, graph algorithms, coding, and distributed computation. We further examine applications in wireless and mobile networks, cyber-physical and healthcare systems, malware and biometric security, scientific computing, and social and biological data analysis. Across these areas, we identify common design principles, including adaptive resource allocation, prediction, message passing, hierarchical representations, and explicit modeling of uncertainty and interactions. The comparison highlights the trade-offs among accuracy, computational cost, communication overhead, privacy, interpretability, and reliability. We conclude by outlining open directions for integrating learning with formal guarantees, scalable hardware and infrastructure, secure data handling, and human-centered evaluation in complex real-world environments.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose an efficient online multi-object tracking framework based on the GMPHD filter and occlusion group management scheme where the GMPHD filter utilizes hierarchical data association to reduce the false negatives caused by miss detection. The hierarchical data association consists of two steps: detection-to-track and track-to-track associations, which can recover the lost tracks and their switched IDs. In addition, the proposed framework is equipped with an object grouping management scheme which handles occlusion problems with two main parts. The first part is "track merging" which can merge the false positive tracks caused by false positive detections from occlusions, where the false positive tracks are usually occluded with a measure. The measure is the occlusion ratio between visual objects, sum-of-intersection-over-area (SIOA) we defined instead of the IOU metric. The second part is "occlusion group energy minimization (OGEM)" which prevents the occluded true positive tracks from false "track merging". We define each group of the occluded objects as an energy function and find an optimal hypothesis which makes the energy minimal. We evaluate the proposed tracker in benchmark datasets such as MOT15 and MOT17 which are built for multi-person tracking. An ablation study in training dataset shows that not only "track merging" and "OGEM" complement each other but also the proposed tracking method has more robust performance and less sensitive to parameters than baseline methods. Also, SIOA works better than IOU for various sizes of false positives. Experimental results show that the proposed tracker efficiently handles occlusion situations and achieves competitive performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods. Especially, our method shows the best multi-object tracking accuracy among the online and real-time executable methods.
generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for navigating and analyzing heterogeneous scientific literature through citation networks and content-based representations. The framework combines graph-based similarity, semantic embeddings, dimensionality reduction, and diversity-aware ranking to identify related work across disciplinary and terminological boundaries. A query-reformulation module iteratively refines user interests from retrieved documents, while a network-based propagation procedure highlights influential and structurally central publications. To improve robustness, we incorporate uncertainty estimates, sampling-based validation, and fairness-aware evaluation, reducing the risk that highly cited or institutionally dominant work overwhelms less visible but relevant contributions. The system supports exploratory tasks including literature search, thematic clustering, citation recommendation, and discovery of emerging research areas. We evaluate it on collections spanning machine learning, optimization, computer systems, social science, medicine, and the humanities, using retrieval accuracy, diversity, coverage, and user-oriented measures. Results show that combining textual and structural evidence consistently outperforms either source alone, particularly for interdisciplinary queries and long-tail topics. Qualitative studies further indicate that interactive reformulation and visual network summaries help users understand relationships among methods, applications, and theoretical results. The framework offers a practical basis for transparent, scalable, and reproducible scholarly knowledge discovery.

original_abstract: While deep learning in 3D domain has achieved revolutionary performance in many tasks, the robustness of these models has not been sufficiently studied or explored. Regarding the 3D adversarial samples, most existing works focus on manipulation of local points, which may fail to invoke the global geometry properties, like robustness under linear projection that preserves the Euclidean distance, i.e., isometry. In this work, we show that existing state-of-the-art deep 3D models are extremely vulnerable to isometry transformations. Armed with the Thompson Sampling, we develop a black-box attack with success rate over 95\% on ModelNet40 data set. Incorporating with the Restricted Isometry Property, we propose a novel framework of white-box attack on top of spectral norm based perturbation. In contrast to previous works, our adversarial samples are experimentally shown to be strongly transferable. Evaluated on a sequence of prevailing 3D models, our white-box attack achieves success rates from 98.88\% to 100\%. It maintains a successful attack rate over 95\% even within an imperceptible rotation range $[\pm 2.81^{\circ}]$.
generated_abstract: This paper presents an interdisciplinary review of contemporary computational intelligence methods and their applications across large-scale data analysis, machine learning, optimization, robotics, communications, language processing, and networked systems. We organize recent approaches according to their principal challenges: learning from limited or noisy information, exploiting structure, improving computational efficiency, and integrating domain knowledge into automated decision making. The review covers advances in sparse and nonlinear representation learning, deep and reinforcement learning, adaptive sequential decision making, compressed and parallel data structures, and optimization methods for discrete and continuous problems. Particular attention is given to mechanisms that improve scalability and reliability, including variance reduction, modular architectures, active learning, structured regularization, graph-based modeling, and hardware-aware computation. We also discuss applications in medical imaging, autonomous navigation, social and biological network analysis, wireless systems, transportation, and scientific instrumentation. Across these domains, we identify recurring trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, robustness, resource consumption, and flexibility. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges in combining symbolic and statistical reasoning, transferring models across changing environments, and designing intelligent systems that can operate efficiently and safely in real-world settings.

original_abstract: A single-point feature has shown its effectiveness in object detection. However, for instance segmentation, it does not lead to satisfactory results. The reasons are two folds. Firstly, it has limited representation capacity. Secondly, it could be misaligned with potential instances. To address the above issues, we propose a new point-based framework, namely PointINS, to segment instances from single points. The core module of our framework is instance-aware convolution, including the instance-agnostic feature and instance-aware weights. Instance-agnostic feature for each Point-of-Interest (PoI) serves as a template for potential instance masks. In this way, instance-aware features are computed by convolving this template with instance-aware weights for following mask prediction. Given the independence of instance-aware convolution, PointINS is general and practical as a one-stage detector for anchor-based and anchor-free frameworks. In our extensive experiments, we show the effectiveness of our framework on RetinaNet and FCOS. With ResNet101 backbone, PointINS achieves 38.3 mask mAP on challenging COCO dataset, outperforming its competitors by a large margin. The code will be made publicly available.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly applied across disciplines, from computer vision, speech and language processing to wireless communications, robotics, healthcare, biology, materials science and cybersecurity. However, this rapid expansion has produced a fragmented body of work, with methods and evaluation practices that are difficult to compare across domains. This paper presents a cross-disciplinary review of data-driven and intelligent computational approaches, emphasizing the relationship between model design, available data, system constraints and application goals. We organize existing research around several recurring themes: representation learning, structured and topological modeling, sequential inference, optimization and game-theoretic decision making, distributed and energy-efficient computation, and robustness, fairness and security. We compare the benefits and limitations of deep, probabilistic, evolutionary and symbolic techniques, while also considering practical issues including interpretability, scalability, privacy, resource consumption and uncertainty. The review identifies common principles underlying successful systems, such as exploiting domain structure, combining heterogeneous information sources and adapting models to deployment conditions. We conclude by outlining open challenges in trustworthy evaluation, reproducibility, human oversight and the integration of learning with physical, social and networked environments.

original_abstract: To increase productivity, today's compilers offer a two-fold abstraction: they hide hardware complexity from the software developer, and they support many architectures and programming languages. At the same time, due to fierce market competition, most processor vendors do not disclose many of their implementation details. These factors force software developers to treat both compilers and architectures as black boxes. In practice, this leads to a suboptimal compiler behavior where the maximum potential of improving an application's resource usage, such as execution time, is often not realized. This paper exposes missed optimization opportunities and is of interest to all three communities, compiler engineers, software developers and hardware architects. By exploiting the behavior of the standard optimization levels, such as the -O3, of the LLVM v6.0 compiler, we show how to reveal hidden cross-architecture and architecture-dependent potential optimizations on two popular processors: the Intel i5-6300U, widely used in portable PCs, and the ARM Cortex-A53-based Broadcom BCM2837 used in the Raspberry Pi 3B+. The classic nightly regression testing can then be extended to use the resource usage and compilation information collected while exploiting subsequences of the standard optimization levels. This provides a systematic means of detecting and tracking missed optimization opportunities. The enhanced nightly regression system is capable of driving the improvement and tuning of the compiler's common optimizer
generated_abstract: Computational research increasingly combines machine learning, embedded systems, simulation, mathematical modeling, and data-intensive workflows, yet the resulting evidence is often difficult to reproduce, evaluate, or safely reuse. This paper presents a framework for trustworthy computational science that treats reproducibility as a property of the entire research lifecycle rather than of source code alone. We identify four complementary requirements: transparent specification of models and assumptions, executable and portable implementations, systematic validation against data and alternative methods, and preservation of provenance, uncertainty, and security information. Drawing on examples ranging from neural-network security and autonomous drone fleets to autoformalization, compressive sensing, hybrid biological models, anonymized networks, financial processes, and geometric statistics, we show how failures in any one layer can undermine scientific conclusions. We discuss practical mechanisms including functional and modular programming, scalable cloud execution, benchmark datasets, adversarial testing, containerized environments, preregistration, and open sharing of data and materials. The framework also emphasizes human-readable explanations and domain-specific validation. Together, these practices can improve the credibility, portability, and long-term value of computational models while supporting responsible innovation across scientific and engineering disciplines.

original_abstract: We address the challenging problem of generating facial attributes using a single image in an unconstrained pose. In contrast to prior works that largely consider generation on 2D near-frontal images, we propose a GAN-based framework to generate attributes directly on a dense 3D representation given by UV texture and position maps, resulting in photorealistic, geometrically-consistent and identity-preserving outputs. Starting from a self-occluded UV texture map obtained by applying an off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction method, we propose two novel components. First, a texture completion generative adversarial network (TC-GAN) completes the partial UV texture map. Second, a 3D attribute generation GAN (3DA-GAN) synthesizes the target attribute while obtaining an appearance consistent with 3D face geometry and preserving identity. Extensive experiments on CelebA, LFW and IJB-A show that our method achieves consistently better attribute generation accuracy than prior methods, a higher degree of qualitative photorealism and preserves face identity information.
generated_abstract: We present an approach for reconstructing missing scientific abstracts from the bibliographic and citation information available in scholarly documents. The method represents each cited publication through its title, abstract, disciplinary concepts, and citation relationships, and combines these heterogeneous signals with a neural text-generation model. A hierarchical encoder captures both local evidence from individual references and global evidence from the distribution of cited work, while a coverage mechanism reduces repetition and encourages the generated text to reflect the paper’s methodological and application-oriented contributions. We evaluate the approach on a large collection of scientific articles spanning computer science, engineering, mathematics, medicine, and the social sciences. Experiments compare citation-aware generation with title-only, abstract-retrieval, and generic language-model baselines. The proposed model produces abstracts that are more factually aligned with the cited literature and better capture the target paper’s research scope, methods, and findings. Human assessment indicates improvements in coherence, informativeness, and disciplinary relevance, although precise numerical claims remain difficult to recover without citation contexts or full text. The results demonstrate that citation networks provide a useful source of structured evidence for scientific document reconstruction and scholarly text generation.

original_abstract: In this work we introduce a new self-supervised, semi-parametric approach for synthesizing novel views of a vehicle starting from a single monocular image. Differently from parametric (i.e. entirely learning-based) methods, we show how a-priori geometric knowledge about the object and the 3D world can be successfully integrated into a deep learning based image generation framework. As this geometric component is not learnt, we call our approach semi-parametric. #R##N#In particular, we exploit man-made object symmetry and piece-wise planarity to integrate rich a-priori visual information into the novel viewpoint synthesis process. An Image Completion Network (ICN) is then trained to generate a realistic image starting from this geometric guidance. #R##N#This careful blend between parametric and non-parametric components allows us to i) operate in a real-world scenario, ii) preserve high-frequency visual information such as textures, iii) handle truly arbitrary 3D roto-translations of the input and iv) perform shape transfer to completely different 3D models. Eventually, we show that our approach can be easily complemented with synthetic data and extended to other rigid objects with completely different topology, even in presence of concave structures and holes (e.g. chairs). #R##N#A comprehensive experimental analysis against state-of-the-art competitors shows the efficacy of our method both from a quantitative and a perceptive point of view. #R##N#Supplementary material, animated results, code and data are available at: this https URL
generated_abstract: Online platforms increasingly personalize information, creating a tension between individual relevance and collective well-being. This paper investigates how personalized recommendation can contribute to opinion polarization and proposes a socially aware framework for mitigating that effect without substantially reducing user utility. We model users, items, and interactions as a dynamic network in which preferences and social relationships co-evolve. The framework combines distributed personalization with graph-based influence estimation, content diversity constraints, and an optimization objective that balances predicted relevance, exposure diversity, privacy, and polarization risk. Unlike approaches that treat polarization as a static property of user groups, our method tracks changes in opinion structure and identifies recommendations likely to reinforce isolated communities or partisan narratives. We evaluate the approach on simulated interaction networks and real-world social media data, including politically sensitive discussions. Results show that modest diversification and influence-aware reranking can significantly reduce polarization and improve cross-group exposure while preserving recommendation quality. The analysis also demonstrates that privacy-preserving, decentralized training is feasible with limited loss in accuracy. These findings suggest that recommender systems should optimize not only immediate engagement, but also the long-term informational health and resilience of online communities.

original_abstract: Deep learning based methods have achieved surprising progress in Scene Text Recognition (STR), one of classic problems in computer vision. In this paper, we propose a feasible framework for multi-lingual arbitrary-shaped STR, including instance segmentation based text detection and language model based attention mechanism for text recognition. Our STR algorithm not only recognizes Latin and Non-Latin characters, but also supports arbitrary-shaped text recognition. Our method wins the championship on Scene Text Spotting Task (Latin Only, Latin and Chinese) of ICDAR2019 Robust Reading Challenge on ArbitraryShaped Text Competition. Code is available at this https URL.

It examines how machine learning, optimization, game theory, probabilistic modeling, formal methods, and network analysis are used to infer latent structure, make predictions, support decisions, and control dynamic environments. Particular attention is given to representation learning, weak and active supervision, uncertainty, causal inference, robustness, interpretability, and efficient computation. The review compares approaches ranging from word and discourse representations to graph-based models, reinforcement learning, deep and spiking neural networks, Bayesian optimization, and symbolic abstractions. Applications include social-media analysis, health monitoring, autonomous driving, wireless-network management, cloud computing, cybersecurity, medical treatment planning, and remote sensing. Across these domains, recurring challenges include incomplete or noisy observations, changing environments, privacy and safety requirements, computational cost, and the need for theoretically justified guarantees. We identify common methodological principles and discuss how combining statistical learning with domain knowledge, structural constraints, and human feedback can improve reliability, efficiency, and transparency. The paper concludes with open research directions for building adaptive, interpretable, and trustworthy intelligent systems.

original_abstract: Recent efforts show that neural networks are vulnerable to small but intentional perturbations on input features in visual classification tasks. Due to the additional consideration of connections between examples (\eg articles with citation link tend to be in the same class), graph neural networks could be more sensitive to the perturbations, since the perturbations from connected examples exacerbate the impact on a target example. Adversarial Training (AT), a dynamic regularization technique, can resist the worst-case perturbations on input features and is a promising choice to improve model robustness and generalization. However, existing AT methods focus on standard classification, being less effective when training models on graph since it does not model the impact from connected examples.  In this work, we explore adversarial training on graph, aiming to improve the robustness and generalization of models learned on graph. We propose Graph Adversarial Training (GraphAT), which takes the impact from connected examples into account when learning to construct and resist perturbations. We give a general formulation of GraphAT, which can be seen as a dynamic regularization scheme based on the graph structure. To demonstrate the utility of GraphAT, we employ it on a state-of-the-art graph neural network model --- Graph Convolutional Network (GCN). We conduct experiments on two citation graphs (Citeseer and Cora) and a knowledge graph (NELL), verifying the effectiveness of GraphAT which outperforms normal training on GCN by 4.51% in node classification accuracy. Codes are available via: https://github.com/fulifeng/GraphAT.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence systems increasingly combine statistical learning, symbolic reasoning, optimization, perception, and interaction, yet these components are commonly developed and evaluated in isolation. This paper presents a unified perspective on the design of intelligent systems that are data-efficient, computationally scalable, interpretable, and robust under changing conditions. We review representative approaches spanning neural representation learning, multilingual language understanding, grounded perception, probabilistic and possibility-based reasoning, differentiable optimization, graph algorithms, formal verification, and secure computation. Particular attention is given to the interface between learning and decision making: models should not merely predict intermediate quantities, but should optimize task-relevant objectives while accounting for uncertainty, constraints, latency, and resource consumption. We further discuss practical requirements for deployment, including adversarial robustness, out-of-distribution behavior, explainability, privacy, software testing, and release management. Across application domains such as robotics, communications, cybersecurity, healthcare, transportation, and education, we identify recurring methodological challenges and opportunities for integration. The paper concludes with research priorities for building AI systems whose capabilities can be measured not only by accuracy, but also by reliability, efficiency, transparency, and their ability to support human decisions.

original_abstract: Executable semantic parsing is the task of converting natural language utterances into logical forms that can be directly used as queries to get a response. We build a transfer learning framework for executable semantic parsing. We show that the framework is effective for Question Answering (QA we experiment with public data sets such as Overnight and NLmaps as well as with commercial SLU data. The experiments carried out on data sets that are different in nature show how executable semantic parsing can unify different areas of NLP such as Q&A and SLU.
generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for discovering, organizing, and explaining relationships among heterogeneous scientific publications. The approach represents papers as a multiplex graph that combines citation links, textual semantics, methodological characteristics, datasets, and application domains. A hierarchical embedding model integrates these complementary signals while preserving both local citation structure and broader conceptual similarity. To improve interpretability, the framework identifies influential concepts, methodological dependencies, and citation pathways, and generates concise summaries adapted to the reader’s background. We further introduce a complexity-aware ranking mechanism that balances relevance, novelty, credibility, and explanatory value when recommending related work. Experiments on multidisciplinary collections show that combining structural and semantic information substantially improves retrieval, clustering, and link prediction compared with text-only and citation-only baselines. Ablation studies demonstrate the contribution of graph structure, contextual features, and audience-aware summarization. The framework also supports temporal analysis, enabling detection of emerging research themes and shifts in methodological practice. These results suggest that integrating graph learning with interpretable language processing can provide a practical foundation for literature exploration, cross-domain knowledge discovery, and more transparent scholarly recommendation systems.

original_abstract: We are witnessing a confluence of vision, speech and dialog system technologies that are enabling the IVAs to learn audio-visual groundings of utterances and have conversations with users about the objects, activities and events surrounding them. Recent progress in visual grounding techniques and Audio Understanding are enabling machines to understand shared semantic concepts and listen to the various sensory events in the environment. With audio and visual grounding methods, end-to-end multimodal SDS are trained to meaningfully communicate with us in natural language about the real dynamic audio-visual sensory world around us. In this work, we explore the role of `topics' as the context of the conversation along with multimodal attention into such an end-to-end audio-visual scene-aware dialog system architecture. We also incorporate an end-to-end audio classification ConvNet, AclNet, into our models. We develop and test our approaches on the Audio Visual Scene-Aware Dialog (AVSD) dataset released as a part of the DSTC7. We present the analysis of our experiments and show that some of our model variations outperform the baseline system released for AVSD.

We further consider algorithmic techniques for reducing communication and query costs, bounding interference in parallel systems, verifying software behavior, and assessing the consequences of structural changes in data and models. Across applications including computer vision, networked storage, epidemiology, scientific measurement, and online information environments, we identify recurring challenges: distribution shift, hidden bias, uncertainty, temporal variation, and the tension between accuracy and computational cost. The analysis suggests that robust performance depends not on a single modeling paradigm, but on integrating statistical learning with explicit constraints, domain knowledge, and empirical validation. We conclude with practical principles for constructing adaptable computational pipelines that remain interpretable, efficient, and dependable as operating conditions change.

original_abstract: Implicit discourse relation recognition is a challenging task due to the absence of the necessary informative clue from explicit connectives. The prediction of relations requires a deep understanding of the semantic meanings of sentence pairs. As implicit discourse relation recognizer has to carefully tackle the semantic similarity of the given sentence pairs and the severe data sparsity issue exists in the meantime, it is supposed to be beneficial from mastering the entire training data. Thus in this paper, we propose a novel memory mechanism to tackle the challenges for further performance improvement. The memory mechanism is adequately memorizing information by pairing representations and discourse relations of all training instances, which right fills the slot of the data-hungry issue in the current implicit discourse relation recognizer. Our experiments show that our full model with memorizing the entire training set reaches new state-of-the-art against strong baselines, which especially for the first time exceeds the milestone of 60% accuracy in the 4-way task.
generated_abstract: Scientific literature is increasingly characterized by rapid growth, disciplinary fragmentation, and complex networks of conceptual and methodological connections. This paper presents a unified framework for analyzing heterogeneous research knowledge through citation contexts, combining semantic representations of text with structural information from citation, collaboration, and topic networks. The approach identifies the roles that references play in scholarly argumentation, distinguishes foundational, methodological, comparative, and application-oriented citations, and detects links between communities that are distant in conventional subject classifications. We evaluate the framework on a broad collection of publications spanning computer science, engineering, mathematics, social science, medicine, and the humanities. Experiments show that incorporating citation context and higher-order network features improves the identification of related work, prediction of emerging connections, and discovery of interdisciplinary research themes compared with methods based only on titles, abstracts, or bibliographic coupling. The analysis also reveals that influential publications may connect otherwise weakly linked areas without being highly similar at the vocabulary level. These results demonstrate the value of combining language and network structure for literature discovery, research evaluation, and the construction of more informative scientific knowledge maps.

original_abstract: The redundancy is widely recognized in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which enables to remove unimportant filters from convolutional layers so as to slim the network with acceptable performance drop. Inspired by the linear and combinational properties of convolution, we seek to make some filters increasingly close and eventually identical for network slimming. To this end, we propose Centripetal SGD (C-SGD), a novel optimization method, which can train several filters to collapse into a single point in the parameter hyperspace. When the training is completed, the removal of the identical filters can trim the network with NO performance loss, thus no finetuning is needed. By doing so, we have partly solved an open problem of constrained filter pruning on CNNs with complicated structure, where some layers must be pruned following others. Our experimental results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet have justified the effectiveness of C-SGD-based filter pruning. Moreover, we have provided empirical evidences for the assumption that the redundancy in deep neural networks helps the convergence of training by showing that a redundant CNN trained using C-SGD outperforms a normally trained counterpart with the equivalent width.

To improve robustness, the framework incorporates uncertainty estimates, temporal information, and explicit modeling of interdisciplinary links. We evaluate the system on a large collection spanning communications, machine learning, computer vision, databases, algorithms, biomedical imaging, and social science. Results show that combining structural and semantic signals substantially improves retrieval and clustering over citation-only and text-only baselines. A user study further indicates that generated summaries help researchers locate transferable methods and understand connections between apparently unrelated fields. We release the annotated benchmark, extraction pipeline, and evaluation scripts to support reproducible research. The proposed framework offers a practical foundation for literature exploration, cross-domain knowledge synthesis, and accelerated scientific discovery.

original_abstract: Modern object detectors can rarely achieve short training time, fast inference speed, and high accuracy at the same time. To strike a balance among them, we propose the Training-Time-Friendly Network (TTFNet). In this work, we start with light-head, single-stage, and anchor-free designs, which enable fast inference speed. Then, we focus on shortening training time. We notice that encoding more training samples from annotated boxes plays a similar role as increasing batch size, which helps enlarge the learning rate and accelerate the training process. To this end, we introduce a novel approach using Gaussian kernels to encode training samples. Besides, we design the initiative sample weights for better information utilization. Experiments on MS COCO show that our TTFNet has great advantages in balancing training time, inference speed, and accuracy. It has reduced training time by more than seven times compared to previous real-time detectors while maintaining state-of-the-art performances. In addition, our super-fast version of TTFNet-18 and TTFNet-53 can outperform SSD300 and YOLOv3 by less than one-tenth of their training time, respectively. The code has been made available at \url{https://github.com/ZJULearning/ttfnet}.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a broad review of computational methods that combine artificial intelligence, machine learning, optimization, and mathematical modeling across diverse application domains. We organize recent work into four themes: learning and inference, structured data analysis, intelligent decision making, and efficient computation. The review covers neural and reinforcement-learning architectures, biologically plausible training, language and vision systems, anomaly detection, medical diagnosis, robotics, communication networks, and social and transportation analysis. We also examine complementary algorithmic foundations, including approximation algorithms, graph kernels, sparse representations, algebraic computation, coding, and information-theoretic methods. Particular attention is given to how model design, representation, external knowledge, human feedback, and domain constraints influence accuracy, efficiency, robustness, and interpretability. Across these areas, empirical improvements often depend as much on data quality, evaluation protocols, and problem formulation as on architectural novelty. We identify recurring challenges, including generalization under distribution shift, reliable uncertainty estimation, fairness, privacy, scalability, and reproducibility. Finally, we outline opportunities for integrating symbolic structure with data-driven learning and for developing evaluation frameworks that compare methods consistently across domains.

original_abstract: Neuromorphic computing takes inspiration from the brain to create energy efficient hardware for information processing, capable of highly sophisticated tasks. In this article, we make the case that building this new hardware necessitates reinventing electronics. We show that research in physics and material science will be key to create artificial nano-neurons and synapses, to connect them together in huge numbers, to organize them in complex systems, and to compute with them efficiently. We describe how some researchers choose to take inspiration from artificial intelligence to move forward in this direction, whereas others prefer taking inspiration from neuroscience, and we highlight recent striking results obtained with these two approaches. Finally, we discuss the challenges and perspectives in neuromorphic physics, which include developing the algorithms and the hardware hand in hand, making significant advances with small toy systems, as well as building large scale networks.

The framework supports several tasks, including related-paper retrieval, topic exploration, citation prediction, and identification of emerging connections across research communities. original_abstract: Storage resources and caching techniques permeate almost every area of communication networks today. In the near future, caching is set to play an important role in storage-assisted Internet architectures, information-centric networks, and wireless systems, reducing operating and capital expenditures and improving the services offered to users. In light of the remarkable data traffic growth and the increasing number of rich-media applications, the impact of caching is expected to become even more profound than it is today. Therefore, it is crucial to design these systems in an optimal fashion, ensuring the maximum possible performance and economic benefits from their deployment. To this end, this article presents a collection of detailed models and algorithms, which are synthesized to build a powerful analytical framework for caching optimization.

This paper presents a cross-disciplinary review of recent computational methods, emphasizing the common principles that underlie apparently different applications. We examine supervised, unsupervised, probabilistic, reinforcement, and game-theoretic approaches, together with optimization, graph-based inference, distributed algorithms, and privacy-preserving computation. Particular attention is given to learning from limited, noisy, streaming, or structured data; reducing computational and communication costs; and integrating uncertainty, feedback, and domain knowledge into prediction and control. Across the surveyed applications, performance gains are commonly achieved by combining data-driven models with explicit structural constraints, adaptive resource management, or human interaction. The review identifies recurring methodological trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, scalability, privacy, and transparency, and highlights open challenges in reproducibility, evaluation, and deployment. These observations motivate a unified research agenda for building reliable intelligent systems that operate effectively in complex real-world environments.

original_abstract: Contextual representation models have achieved great success in improving various downstream tasks. However, these language-model-based encoders are difficult to train due to the large parameter sizes and high computational complexity. By carefully examining the training procedure, we find that the softmax layer (the output layer) causes significant inefficiency due to the large vocabulary size. Therefore, we redesign the learning objective and propose an efficient framework for training contextual representation models. Specifically, the proposed approach bypasses the softmax layer by performing language modeling with dimension reduction, and allows the models to leverage pre-trained word embeddings. Our framework reduces the time spent on the output layer to a negligible level, eliminates almost all the trainable parameters of the softmax layer and performs language modeling without truncating the vocabulary. When applied to ELMo, our method achieves a 4 times speedup and eliminates 80% trainable parameters while achieving competitive performance on downstream tasks.

The framework represents heterogeneous observations as compact vector, relational, and probabilistic descriptions, enabling learning from text, images, signals, graphs, and time-dependent sensor data within a common pipeline. It supports automatic extraction of entities, procedures, mathematical relations, and causal hypotheses; uncertainty-aware prediction and domain adaptation; and interaction with formal models for verification, planning, and control. To improve scalability, the framework employs sparse and discrete representations, distributed optimization, hashing, and accelerated numerical computation. Its modular design also permits deployment across cloud, edge, and embedded platforms, while privacy-sensitive data can be minimized or processed locally. We demonstrate the approach on representative tasks including scientific knowledge extraction, multimodal recognition, anomaly detection, human activity monitoring, network analysis, and autonomous decision making. Across these settings, the proposed combination of learned representations and explicit structure improves interpretability, computational efficiency, and robustness compared with isolated black-box models. The results suggest that integrating compression, reasoning, and adaptive learning provides a practical route toward versatile intelligent systems capable of operating under incomplete, noisy, and changing information.

original_abstract: We develop new abstractions for reasoning about three relaxations of differential privacy:  $R$ enyi differential privacy, zero-concentrated differential privacy, and truncated concentrated differential privacy, which express bounds on statistical divergences between two output probability distributions. In order to reason about such properties compositionally, we introduce approximate span-lifting, a novel construction extending the approximate relational lifting approaches previously developed for standard differential privacy to a more general class of divergences, and also to continuous distributions. As an application, we develop a program logic based on approximate span-liftings capable of proving relaxations of differential privacy and other statistical divergence properties.
generated_abstract: Intelligent systems operating in real-world environments must combine incomplete knowledge, uncertain observations, learned models, and the actions of multiple interacting agents. This paper presents an integrated framework for decision making under such conditions. The framework represents beliefs about dynamic worlds symbolically and probabilistically, while attaching provenance and argumentative evidence to observations, predictions, and conclusions. Neural components are used for classification, sequence labeling, fault diagnosis, and state estimation, with uncertainty information explicitly propagated so that unknown or weakly supported features do not produce unjustified decisions. A cooperation layer determines when a task cannot be solved by an individual agent and identifies the coordination required among heterogeneous or homogeneous agents. For continuous systems, the framework supports feedback synchronization and uncertainty-aware tracking of nonlinear, maneuvering targets. Efficient temporal queries and scalable provenance storage enable reasoning over high-volume streams without requiring exhaustive inference. We formalize the interfaces between perception, belief revision, planning, coordination, and control, and illustrate their use in representative networked, robotic, and cyber-physical scenarios. The results show that combining structured evidence with probabilistic and learning-based methods improves robustness, interpretability, and timely response in dynamic uncertain environments.

original_abstract: There is a growing interest in learning a model which could recognize novel classes with only a few labeled examples. In this paper, we propose Temporal Alignment Module (TAM), a novel few-shot learning framework that can learn to classify a previous unseen video. While most previous works neglect long-term temporal ordering information, our proposed model explicitly leverages the temporal ordering information in video data through temporal alignment. This leads to strong data-efficiency for few-shot learning. In concrete, TAM calculates the distance value of query video with respect to novel class proxies by averaging the per frame distances along its alignment path. We introduce continuous relaxation to TAM so the model can be learned in an end-to-end fashion to directly optimize the few-shot learning objective. We evaluate TAM on two challenging real-world datasets, Kinetics and Something-Something-V2, and show that our model leads to significant improvement of few-shot video classification over a wide range of competitive baselines.
generated_abstract: We present a unified computational framework for analyzing and solving complex decision, estimation, and prediction problems arising in networked and autonomous systems. The framework combines graph-based representations, statistical learning, optimization, game theory, and control, allowing heterogeneous information and domain constraints to be incorporated within a common methodology. We develop models for relational inference, resource allocation, privacy-preserving data analysis, trajectory planning, multi-agent interaction, and adaptive system operation. Particular attention is given to computational efficiency: scalable relaxations, approximation algorithms, structured prediction, pruning, and offline–online decompositions are used to support real-time deployment. The approach also accommodates uncertainty and incomplete observations through probabilistic modeling, contextual information, and interactive human feedback. We evaluate the resulting methods on applications including semantic networks, recommender systems, conversational and behavioral analysis, imaging, robotics, wireless communication, and infrastructure control. Across these settings, the experiments demonstrate that exploiting global structure and interactions can improve accuracy, robustness, energy efficiency, and interpretability compared with isolated local models. The results highlight the value of integrating learning and decision-making for understanding and managing complex technological and social systems.

original_abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have shown huge superiority over humans in image recognition, speech processing, autonomous vehicles and medical diagnosis. However, recent studies indicate that DNNs are vulnerable to adversarial examples (AEs), which are designed by attackers to fool deep learning models. Different from real examples, AEs can mislead the model to predict incorrect outputs while hardly be distinguished by human eyes, therefore threaten security-critical deep-learning applications. In recent years, the generation and defense of AEs have become a research hotspot in the field of artificial intelligence (AI) security. This article reviews the latest research progress of AEs. First, we introduce the concept, cause, characteristics and evaluation metrics of AEs, then give a survey on the state-of-the-art AE generation methods with the discussion of advantages and disadvantages. After that, we review the existing defenses and discuss their limitations. Finally, future research opportunities and challenges on AEs are prospected.

The framework emphasizes how structured representations, efficient inference, robustness, and distributed computation enable reliable performance under limited, noisy, incomplete, or adversarial information. We organize existing approaches according to the type of structure they exploit, including graphs, spatial and temporal relationships, hierarchical representations, probabilistic dependencies, and domain-specific constraints. We discuss applications ranging from language processing, recommendation, computer vision, medical imaging, robotics, and reinforcement learning to communication systems, smart grids, blockchain, and scientific data management. Across these settings, we identify recurring design principles: combining complementary information sources, adapting computation to sparsity and hardware constraints, enforcing consistency or privacy, and integrating uncertainty into decision making. We further highlight the importance of interpretable models, reproducible datasets, and theoretically grounded evaluation, particularly when systems operate in safety-critical or resource-constrained environments. The resulting synthesis clarifies common methodological connections among seemingly disparate problems and outlines open challenges in scalable learning, robust optimization, autonomous adaptation, and trustworthy deployment.

original_abstract: Although deep neural networks have been successful in image classification, they are prone to adversarial attacks. To generate misclassified inputs, there has emerged a wide variety of techniques, such as black- and whitebox testing of neural networks. In this paper, we present DeepSearch, a novel blackbox-fuzzing technique for image classifiers. Despite its simplicity, DeepSearch is shown to be more effective in finding adversarial examples than closely related black- and whitebox approaches. DeepSearch is additionally able to generate the most subtle adversarial examples in comparison to these approaches.
generated_abstract: Graphs provide a natural language for representing relationships in data, yet the rapid growth of graph-based methods has produced a fragmented body of work spanning algorithms, machine learning, network science, geometry, and real-world applications. This paper presents a broad review of computational techniques for learning from and reasoning over graphs. We organize existing approaches according to graph structure, learning objective, and computational setting, covering graph construction, representation learning, community detection, graphical models, dynamic and multilayer networks, geometric queries, optimization, and scalable parallel processing. We discuss both classical methods and recent neural architectures, including convolutional, recurrent, attention-based, and embedding-based models, and examine their use in vision, language, recommendation, health, sensing, robotics, transportation, and online social systems. Particular attention is given to scalability, uncertainty, robustness, interpretability, temporal dynamics, and the integration of heterogeneous data sources. Through comparisons of representative methods and application studies, we identify recurring trade-offs between accuracy, computational cost, data requirements, and theoretical guarantees. We conclude by outlining open problems in benchmark design, reproducibility, privacy, adaptive graph learning, and the development of unified methods capable of exploiting structure across domains.

original_abstract: We simulate data using a graphic engine to augment real-world datasets, with application to vehicle re-identification (re-ID). In order for data augmentation to be effective, the simulated data should be similar to the real data in key attributes like illumination and viewpoint. We introduce a large-scale synthetic dataset VehicleX. Created in Unity, it contains 1,209 vehicles of various models in 3D with fully editable attributes. We propose an attribute descent approach to let VehicleX approximate the attributes in real-world datasets. Specifically, we manipulate each attribute in VehicleX, aiming to minimize the discrepancy between VehicleX and real data in terms of the Fr'echet Inception Distance (FID). This attribute descent algorithm allows content-level domain adaptation (DA), which has advantages over existing DA methods working on the pixel level or feature level. We mix adapted VehicleX data with three vehicle re-ID datasets individually, and observe consistent improvement when the proposed attribute descent is applied. With the augmented datasets, we report competitive accuracy compared with state-of-the-art results. The VehicleX engine and code of this paper will be released.

original_abstract: Designing a molecule with desired properties is one of the biggest challenges in drug development, as it requires optimization of chemical compound structures with respect to many complex properties. To augment the compound design process we introduce Mol-CycleGAN - a CycleGAN-based model that generates optimized compounds with high structural similarity to the original ones. Namely, given a molecule our model generates a structurally similar one with an optimized value of the considered property. We evaluate the performance of the model on selected optimization objectives related to structural properties (presence of halogen groups, number of aromatic rings) and to a physicochemical property (penalized logP). In the task of optimization of penalized logP of drug-like molecules our model significantly outperforms previous results.
generated_abstract: Modern scientific and engineering problems increasingly require methods that integrate network structure, statistical learning, optimization, and human behavior. This paper presents a unified perspective on data-driven decision making in complex systems, emphasizing how information is represented, propagated, inferred, and acted upon under uncertainty. We review representative advances in social and biological diffusion, distributed detection, wireless cooperation, market mechanisms, and software systems, and relate them to contemporary approaches in compressive estimation, medical image analysis, learned compression, generative modeling, and passive three-dimensional imaging. Across these domains, we identify recurring principles: exploiting structured representations, selecting informative or fair interactions, combining local decisions hierarchically, and designing objectives that reflect application-specific performance rather than surrogate error alone. We also discuss the role of controlled datasets, interpretable evaluation metrics, and computational tools that can translate complex observations into reliable decisions. Particular attention is given to robustness under distribution shift, unpaired or incomplete data, and socially consequential bias. The resulting framework highlights both the promise and limitations of current methods and outlines directions for developing transparent, efficient, and generalizable computational systems that connect algorithmic innovation with real-world scientific and societal needs.

original_abstract: Land cover classification of remote sensing images is a challenging task due to limited amounts of annotated data, highly imbalanced classes, frequent incorrect pixel-level annotations, and an inherent complexity in the semantic segmentation task. In this article, we propose a novel architecture called the dense dilated convolutions' merging network (DDCM-Net) to address this task. The proposed DDCM-Net consists of dense dilated image convolutions merged with varying dilation rates. This effectively utilizes rich combinations of dilated convolutions that enlarge the network's receptive fields with fewer parameters and features compared with the state-of-the-art approaches in the remote sensing domain. Importantly, DDCM-Net obtains fused local- and global-context information, in effect incorporating surrounding discriminative capability for multiscale and complex-shaped objects with similar color and textures in very high-resolution aerial imagery. We demonstrate the effectiveness, robustness, and flexibility of the proposed DDCM-Net on the publicly available ISPRS Potsdam and Vaihingen data sets, as well as the DeepGlobe land cover data set. Our single model, trained on three-band Potsdam and Vaihingen data sets, achieves better accuracy in terms of both mean intersection over union (mIoU) and F1-score compared with other published models trained with more than three-band data. We further validate our model on the DeepGlobe data set, achieving state-of-the-art result 56.2% mIoU with much fewer parameters and at a lower computational cost compared with related recent work. Code available at https://github.com/samleoqh/DDCM-Semantic-Segmentation-PyTorch
generated_abstract: This paper presents a unified framework for designing intelligent, adaptive, and trustworthy cyber-physical systems that operate across heterogeneous sensing, communication, computation, and decision-making environments. The framework combines distributed Internet of Things architectures with cloud, fog, and edge services; machine learning methods for perception, prediction, and control; and formal approaches for verification, correctness, privacy, and fairness. Particular attention is given to the challenges created by resource-constrained devices, correlated and time-varying data, uncertain human preferences, and the need to protect both observations and learned models. The proposed architecture separates sensing, machine interaction, user interaction, and supervisory services, enabling modular deployment and reducing unnecessary communication and computational overhead. Learning components are augmented with interpretable attribution methods, equitable personalization mechanisms, and safety constraints that can be checked before execution. We discuss how the framework supports applications including elderly care, smart grids, robotic manipulation, remote sensing, education, and autonomous mobility. Through conceptual analysis and representative computational experiments, we show that combining adaptive learning with distributed optimization and formal assurance can improve efficiency and robustness without sacrificing privacy or human oversight. The results establish design principles for dependable intelligent systems operating in complex real-world environments.

original_abstract: Reconstructing 3D human shape and pose from a monocular image is challenging despite the promising results achieved by the most recent learning-based methods. The commonly occurred misalignment comes from the facts that the mapping from images to the model space is highly non-linear and the rotation-based pose representation of the body model is prone to result in the drift of joint positions. In this work, we investigate learning 3D human shape and pose from dense correspondences of body parts and propose a Decompose-and-aggregate Network (DaNet) to address these issues. DaNet adopts the dense correspondence maps, which densely build a bridge between 2D pixels and 3D vertexes, as intermediate representations to facilitate the learning of 2D-to-3D mapping. The prediction modules of DaNet are decomposed into one global stream and multiple local streams to enable global and fine-grained perceptions for the shape and pose predictions, respectively. Messages from local streams are further aggregated to enhance the robust prediction of the rotation-based poses, where a position-aided rotation feature refinement strategy is proposed to exploit spatial relationships between body joints. Moreover, a Part-based Dropout (PartDrop) strategy is introduced to drop out dense information from intermediate representations during training, encouraging the network to focus on more complementary body parts as well as adjacent position features. The effectiveness of our method is validated on both in-door and real-world datasets including the Human3.6M, UP3D, and DensePose-COCO datasets. Experimental results show that the proposed method significantly improves the reconstruction performance in comparison with previous state-of-the-art methods.
