generated_abstract: We present a unified framework for organizing, discovering, and analyzing heterogeneous scientific knowledge from scholarly documents. The framework combines unsupervised concept extraction, semantic representation learning, graph-based modeling, and task-oriented recommendation to connect methods, applications, datasets, and findings across disciplines. Scientific titles and abstracts are processed to identify typed concepts without relying on domain-specific ontologies, while neural and probabilistic models capture relations among concepts, authors, papers, and research communities. A multilayer knowledge graph supports semantic search, citation and document recommendation, emerging-topic detection, and exploration of methodological links between otherwise disconnected fields. To improve robustness, the framework incorporates domain generalization, interpretable representations, uncertainty estimation, and scalable online learning, enabling adaptation to new corpora and rapidly changing research areas. We evaluate the approach on large collections spanning computer science, engineering, medicine, and the social sciences. Results show that combining textual, structural, and temporal evidence improves concept quality, retrieval accuracy, and recommendation performance over content-only and graph-only baselines. The proposed system offers an extensible foundation for building academic knowledge bases and for assisting researchers in navigating increasingly interdisciplinary literatures.

original_abstract: We propose a novel text generation task, namely Curiosity-driven Question Generation. We start from the observation that the Question Generation task has traditionally been considered as the dual problem of Question Answering, hence tackling the problem of generating a question given the text that contains its answer. Such questions can be used to evaluate machine reading comprehension. However, in real life, and especially in conversational settings, humans tend to ask questions with the goal of enriching their knowledge and/or clarifying aspects of previously gathered information. We refer to these inquisitive questions as Curiosity-driven: these questions are generated with the goal of obtaining new information (the answer) which is not present in the input text. In this work, we experiment on this new task using a conversational Question Answering (QA) dataset; further, since the majority of QA dataset are not built in a conversational manner, we describe a methodology to derive data for this novel task from non-conversational QA data. We investigate several automated metrics to measure the different properties of Curious Questions, and experiment different approaches on the Curiosity-driven Question Generation task, including model pre-training and reinforcement learning. Finally, we report a qualitative evaluation of the generated outputs.
generated_abstract: This paper presents a systematic survey of computational methods for designing reliable, intelligent, and secure data-driven systems. We organize recent work spanning machine learning, graph analysis, natural-language processing, computer vision, communications, cloud computing, formal methods, and privacy-preserving computation. The review examines how modern systems represent information, learn from incomplete or noisy observations, make decisions under uncertainty, and maintain performance in dynamic environments. Particular attention is given to efficiency and scalability, including compact representations, approximate inference, distributed processing, energy-aware resource management, and algorithms with provable complexity or generalization guarantees. We also analyze robustness and trustworthiness, covering error detection, adversarial resilience, authentication, control-flow protection, differential privacy, secure virtualization, and equitable access to digital services. Across application areas, we identify recurring design principles: combining domain knowledge with data-driven learning, exploiting structure in representations, adapting computation to context, and evaluating both utility and risk. The synthesis highlights open challenges involving reproducibility, interpretability, distribution shift, human effort, and the trade-offs among accuracy, latency, privacy, security, and resource consumption. Finally, we propose a research agenda for integrated, dependable computational systems capable of operating across heterogeneous domains and infrastructure.
